title: Trump's immigration crackdown looms over Minnesota's bruising Senate primary - PBS
description:
Until Craig's Senate run, the heat came from the right.
'I regret my vote,' Craig wrote in a mea culpa Chief among them was the Laken Riley Act, the first bill passed by Congress after Trump started his second term.
Flanagan supporters are suspicious of Craig To Flanagan and her supporters, Craig's vote for the immigration bill was not a pragmatic overture to swing voters but a betrayal.
"My primary opponent voted for Donald Trump's immigration bill and was the only Minnesota Democrat to do so," Flanagan told volunteers in St. Paul on Saturday.
READ MORE: A timeline of Trump's immigration crackdown in Minnesota Like Abdul El-Sayed, who won last week's Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, Flanagan supports Medicare for All and wants to curtail U.S. military support for Israel.
text:
Craig voted for tighter enforcement soon after Trump returned to office last year, only to later express regret for her decision after the Republican president sent a surge of agents into Minneapolis. She backed a resolution that condemned antisemitism after a 2025 firebombing in Boulder, Colorado, and expressed thanks for law enforcement, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers.

Those votes may turn out to be some of the most fraught of Craig's eight-year career in Congress, decisions that Flanagan has highlighted while trying to portray her rival as unwilling to fight an unpopular administration in Washington.

"I think that's when she lost my vote permanently and that's why I will not vote for her no matter what," said Bryce Bohne, 40, of Minneapolis. The teacher and owner of an educational tourism company is supporting Flanagan.

Around the Whipple federal building, the fences and barriers are down. The ambient soundtrack is no longer the whistles and chants of protesters, just the rumble of departing jets and passing buses.

But the signs of what happened remain. A few volunteers in bright orange vests keep vigil across the street for 12-plus hours a day, ready to help people getting released from immigration detention or leaving hearings at the immigration court inside.

A few miles away, visitors still bring fresh flowers and handwritten notes to memorials marking the spots where Renee Good and Alex Pretti were killed.

Craig is no stranger to tough races, but until now the heat was from the right

Craig flipped a Republican-held seat in 2018, and every two years she overcame millions of dollars of attack ads to win tough reelection campaigns.

Until Craig's Senate run, the heat came from the right. Newly under fire from the other side, the decisions she made as a swing-seat congresswoman have become a liability as a statewide Senate candidate. At one recent event, she adopted the language of the insurgent left, though it did not always seem to come naturally.

READ MORE: How Troy Jackson went from Maine logger to Democratic nominee for Senate against Susan Collins

"The working class keeps getting screwed," she told volunteers preparing to knock on doors for her Saturday in Brooklyn Park, a Minneapolis suburb. "Folks, I don't know about you, but it is time that we had a working folks reno— reso— renovation—"

Here, she took a breath.

"—revolution in this country."

In Craig's view, she is well suited to the antiestablishment fervor gaining a foothold in the Democratic Party. Raised by a single mother in an Arkansas trailer park, she has known economic hardship. The lesbian mother of four grown children, she is not the archetype of a traditional member of Congress.

She was one of the House Democrats to call for President Joe Biden to drop out of the 2024 race after his disastrous debate performance against Trump. As a relatively junior member of Congress, she pushed successfully to become the top Democrat on the Agriculture Committee, jumping ahead of long-tenured colleagues.

"I consider myself a progressive" she told reporters after her event Saturday. "Every race that I run, Republicans run ads against me saying I vote with Democrats 96, 97% of the time."

"Of course, in the primary," she added, "people want to point out the few votes I've taken against Democrats."

'I regret my vote,' Craig wrote in a mea culpa

Chief among them was the Laken Riley Act, the first bill passed by Congress after Trump started his second term. It requires federal authorities to detain migrants accused of theft and violent crimes.

Craig and nearly 60 other Democrats in the House and Senate voted for the bill early in 2025.

But at the end of the year, as immigration officers descended on Minneapolis, that vote became a liability. Weeks after Good and Pretti were killed, Craig published a mea culpa in a Minnesota Star Tribune column.

WATCH: What El-Sayed's primary win means for Democrats in November

Craig explained that although she had qualms with parts of the law, it had the support of Democrats she respected, and many of her constituents were unhappy with the situation on the border under Biden.

But the "outright occupation by aggressive, unaccountable federal forces" made clear to her "that supporting any bill that gives ICE new authority in this administration was the wrong decision. And I regret my vote."

Trump's immigration operation, she says, was not enabled by her vote on the Laken Riley Act.

"Before that, people had a little bit more sensibility about the fact she was in a tough district and had to take tough votes," said Corey Day, former executive director of the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party.

Craig has since presented herself as a strong defender of Minnesotans against Trump. She says her record of winning tough races positions her to ensure the seat stays in Democratic hands.

"Angie has experience working across demographics that we need to win over statewide, including in rural Minnesota," said Kevin Anderson, a Hennepin County commissioner who is supporting Craig and went to one of her weekend events. "I love Peggy, I really do, she's a great politician. But I don't think she's ever had to work across Minnesota."

Democratic Gov. Tim Walz has declined to endorse either candidate for the seat held by Democrat Tina Smith, who is not running again. Late last month his wife, Gwen Walz, endorsed Craig over Flanagan, his governing partner for two terms.

The Republican field includes Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter.

Flanagan supporters are suspicious of Craig

To Flanagan and her supporters, Craig's vote for the immigration bill was not a pragmatic overture to swing voters but a betrayal.

"My primary opponent voted for Donald Trump's immigration bill and was the only Minnesota Democrat to do so," Flanagan told volunteers in St. Paul on Saturday. "She since then has said that she regrets that vote, and I'm glad. But it shouldn't have taken 14 months."

"We can stand with the immigrant community and not just when it's politically expedient for us," Flanagan added.

READ MORE: A timeline of Trump's immigration crackdown in Minnesota

Like Abdul El-Sayed, who won last week's Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, Flanagan supports Medicare for All and wants to curtail U.S. military support for Israel. She is running as much against the donors who have spent millions of dollars backing Craig as she is against Craig herself.

"The fact that the money is coming from us and only us makes such a huge difference, because she's beholden to us, not some billionaire with some business or crypto interest," said 43-year-old Flanagan supporter Justin Ropella, a customer service manager from Woodbury.

Through July 22, Craig's campaign had spent $9 million and Flanagan's $5.5 million. The disparity was even higher among outside groups, with Craig backers spending considerably more, though both have benefited from an influx of outside spending.

To help make up the difference, Flanagan has called on the support of progressive champions such as Sen. Bernie Sanders the Vermont independent who campaigned with her last month.

"If the people of Minnesota can stand up — and I'm confident that they can — and tell these billionaires and their lies and their 30-second ads and their super PACs to go to hell, democracy is going to reign," Sanders said.

text:
WASHINGTON — New federal data shows more than 835 people were held in solitary confinement each month in immigration detention during the current fiscal year, while detainees identified as seriously ill, suicidal or on hunger strikes spent extended periods in isolation, according to reporting highlighted in a weekly roundup by Solitary Watch.

As reported in the weekly roundup article by Solitary Watch, new ICE data and recent developments highlight the continued use of solitary confinement, including extended isolation, hunger strikes and forced medical treatment.

According to a Daily Beast article spotlighted in the Solitary Watch roundup, which examined ICE data for fiscal year 2026, the average period of uninterrupted solitary confinement for detainees identified as seriously ill, suicidal or on hunger strike was 63 days during the winter quarter.

According to new Immigration and Customs Enforcement data, more than 835 people were held in solitary confinement each month during the current fiscal year, while some detainees classified as seriously ill or suicidal spent an average of 63 consecutive days in isolation.

According to the report, people who have been identified as medically or psychologically vulnerable have been placed in isolation for extended periods of time.

The publication compared that figure with the United Nations standard, which considers prolonged solitary confinement of more than 15 days to be torture under certain conditions.

Solitary confinement, also known as restrictive or segregated housing by federal agencies, is the practice of separating individuals from the rest of the detention population. The conditions vary depending on the facility and the reason for placement.

Apart from that, according to a Government Accountability Office report from 2023, ICE placed detained noncitizens in segregated housing 14,581 times between fiscal years 2017 and 2021.

Approximately 40% of those placements were for disciplinary reasons, with the remaining 60% for administrative reasons such as protective custody and medical considerations.

The GAO also discovered that ICE’s data did not always provide adequate information about why people were placed in segregated housing.

The agency’s records did not always identify detained individuals deemed vulnerable because of medical or mental health issues.

The continued use of solitary confinement has also sparked concern because of the treatment of hunger strikers in immigration detention.

An ICE Health Services document shows that at least one hunger striker was forced to receive medical treatment during the current administration. According to the report, some detainees participating in hunger strikes have been placed in solitary confinement.

Separately, The Guardian reported Aug. 5 that ICE had attempted to subject at least 10 detained immigrants participating in hunger strikes to involuntary medical procedures since 2025.

According to the investigation, at least three people were subjected to the procedures, and up to two more may have received forced treatment. Force-feeding was one of the reported procedures, which involved inserting a tube through the nose into the stomach.

The Guardian’s reporting was based on court records and interviews from multiple immigration detention facilities. According to the publication, many of the detainees involved lacked legal representation during proceedings in which the government sought court authorization for forced medical treatment.

The issue of solitary confinement extends beyond immigration detention.

Highlighted in the Solitary Watch article, the New York Daily News reported the death of Godfrie Cole, a 25-year-old man who died in July while being held in a segregated housing unit at the federal Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn. Authorities suspected a drug overdose, according to the report.

Other cases highlighted by Solitary Watch involved individuals held in restrictive housing for extended periods.

According to The Virginian-Pilot, spotlighted in the Solitary Watch article, Tyquine Lee developed schizophrenia and lost his ability to speak after spending more than 600 days in solitary confinement at Red Onion State Prison in Virginia.

His case helped shape legal and legislative efforts to reform the state’s use of restrictive housing.

Federal oversight agencies have previously expressed concerns about the conditions inside ICE detention facilities.

In 2025, the GAO reported that ICE was responsible for the confinement of more than 37,000 detained noncitizens on an average day during fiscal year 2024 across more than 100 facilities.

The agency discovered flaws in ICE’s inspection and oversight systems and suggested that the Department of Homeland Security establish more specific goals and measures for evaluating detention facilities.

More recent GAO findings show the rapid expansion of ICE detention.

According to a June 2026 report, the average daily ICE detention population increased by 71%, from 39,314 on Jan. 20, 2025, to 67,204 on April 1, 2026.

Similarly, the number of authorized ICE detention facilities increased from 134 to 239 during the same period.

The growing number of people held in immigration detention has focused attention on how facilities use restrictive housing and provide medical care to detainees.

According to ICE’s detention standards, segregated housing is intended to protect detainees, staff and facility security. However, government oversight reports have identified gaps in the agency’s documentation and monitoring of the practice.

The newly released data and recent reporting have reignited debate over how frequently solitary confinement is used in immigration detention and how long vulnerable detainees are isolated.

While ICE maintains segregated housing standards, federal oversight reports and independent investigations have raised ongoing concerns about the agency’s data collection, facility conditions and treatment of those held in isolation.

text:
Inhumane enforcement

“Map Shows ICE Deportation Costs in Every US County,” (modbee.com, Aug. 5)

White House Border Czar Tom Homan predicted “bloodshed” if people are told “not to comply with law enforcement.” Homan made these comments in reference to immigrants who died at the hands of immigration officials, but his framing suggests that the victims themselves are responsible for their own deaths.

The church has long rejected the vilification of law enforcement, but it also rejects the vilification of peaceful protesters who exercise their constitutional rights. To imply that those who raise moral concerns about immigration practices should “shut their mouth,” as Homan put it, is to dismiss legitimate calls for accountability and human dignity.

Homan insists that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is merely enforcing laws enacted by Congress. But Catholic leaders such as Bishop Daniel E. García and Bishop Brendan J. Cahill remind us that the enforcement of any law must be carried out “in a humane manner and with respect for fundamental human rights, including the rights to life and due process.” They call for “accountability, transparency and justice,” and for meaningful reforms to our immigration system.

These concerns are not theoretical. ICE has shot 23 people in the last year, and 32 people died in ICE custody in 2025. This is not what humane enforcement looks like.

Fr Misael Avila

Turlock

Selfish corporate developers

“Modesto contacted by data center developer. MID says it aims to protect ratepayers,” (modbee.com, July 30)

Modesto leaders should not feel obligated to meet with data center developers. These developers should be presenting ideas at public meetings — not behind closed doors.

We don’t have the extra power on the grid for something like this. The Modesto Irrigation District’s grid is mostly reliant on fossil fuels, which is bad for Central Valley air and home electric rates.

I urge the Modesto City Council to decline data center development proposals and any other selfish corporate developers.

Brad Johnson

Salida

Recommit to voting rights

“U.S. Supreme Court lets Voting Rights Act ruling take effect ahead of schedule,” (modbee.com, May 4)

August marks the 61st anniversary of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, a monumental law built on the patriotic principle that every American citizen deserves an unhindered voice in our democracy. Yet, some politicians are supporting the SAVE Act, a federal bill in the House of Representatives that would change how we vote.

The act purports to “save” us from a threat that is almost entirely mythical.

Proponents insist that the act stops noncitizens from casting ballots. But even the conservative Heritage Foundation’s own voter fraud database found fewer than 100 cases of noncitizens voting out of well over a billion votes cast over several decades.

Our problem isn’t noncitizens voting; it’s that roughly 35% to 40% of eligible American citizens don’t vote. Instead of making voting easier, the SAVE Act requires documents — like original birth certificates or passports — that millions of ordinary Americans simply do not have.

Disenfranchising legitimate American voters over a nonexistent problem isn’t voter security, it is un-American, un-patriotic and an insult to our intelligence. Let’s honor the Voting Rights Act by opening the doors to voters and encouraging them to reject the SAVE Act and all of its supporters.

Eric Peterson

Santa Rosa

title: Trump immigration policies divide Republicans and independents - TheGrio
description:
That distinction matters because Americans do not appear to be rejecting immigration enforcement altogether.
Instead, several polls suggest many voters support enforcing immigration laws while questioning how aggressively those laws are being enforced.
Among independents, support for a pathway to citizenship reached 79%.
Independents, however, appear much more skeptical of how deportations and enforcement operations are being carried out, even as many continue to support legal immigration and immigration enforcement more broadly.
With control of Congress at stake, the political question may be less about whether voters support immigration enforcement and more about how far they believe that enforcement should go.
text:
President Donald Trump continues to have strong Republican support for his immigration agenda. But as the 2026 midterm elections approach, polling shows a much different picture among independent voters, particularly when it comes to ICE and the administration’s deportation tactics.

That distinction matters because Americans do not appear to be rejecting immigration enforcement altogether. Instead, several polls suggest many voters support enforcing immigration laws while questioning how aggressively those laws are being enforced.

A Quinnipiac University poll released July 29 found that 60% of registered voters disapproved of the way U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement was doing its job, compared with 37% who approved. The partisan divide was stark: 78% of Republicans approved of ICE, while 94% of Democrats and 67% of independents disapproved.

Those independent voters could be especially important in November.

In the same Quinnipiac poll, independents favored Democratic control of the U.S. House over Republican control, 53% to 31%. Nearly half of independent voters (49%) also said they were more motivated to participate in this year’s midterms than in previous midterms.

The polling does not mean immigration will determine how independents vote. The economy, foreign policy and other issues will also shape the midterms. But the numbers do show a clear gap between Republican and independent voters on one of Trump’s signature issues.

That divide has appeared in other polling as well.

YouGov found in late 2025 that 79% of Republicans approved of ICE’s job performance. Among independents, just 25% approved while 62% disapproved. The same survey found 60% of independents believed ICE’s tactics were too forceful, compared with only 12% of Republicans.

Concerns about ICE also extend beyond partisan politics.

YouGov found that 65% of Black Americans were concerned that someone they knew could be mistreated by ICE. Among Hispanic Americans, that figure rose to 72%.

More recent polling shows similar concerns about deportations.

In April, the Pew Research Center found that 52% of Americans believed the Trump administration was doing too much to deport immigrants living in the country illegally. Thirty-one percent said the administration was doing about the right amount, while 15% said it was doing too little.

Black Americans were more likely than the public overall to say the administration had gone too far. Sixty-nine percent of Black adults said the administration was doing too much on deportations, along with 65% of Hispanic adults and 58% of Asian adults. Among white adults, 45% said the same.

Those numbers are particularly relevant for Black voters as the debate over immigration increasingly raises broader questions about government authority, law enforcement and who may be affected by aggressive enforcement practices.

At the same time, Americans remain broadly positive about immigration itself.

Gallup reported in July that 73% of Americans consider immigration a good thing for the country. While that figure was down from a record-high 79% in 2025, it remained above Gallup’s 25-year average of 67%. Among independents, 73% also viewed immigration positively.

Gallup found more division when voters were asked about specific enforcement policies. Forty-nine percent supported hiring significantly more Border Patrol agents, while 48% opposed it. But 58% opposed deporting all immigrants living in the United States illegally, and 75% supported allowing undocumented immigrants to become citizens if they meet certain requirements. Among independents, support for a pathway to citizenship reached 79%.

Taken together, the polling suggests Americans’ views on immigration are more complicated than a simple divide between those who support enforcement and those who oppose it.

Republicans remain overwhelmingly supportive of Trump’s immigration agenda and ICE. Independents, however, appear much more skeptical of how deportations and enforcement operations are being carried out, even as many continue to support legal immigration and immigration enforcement more broadly.

That creates a potential challenge for Republicans heading into November.

Immigration helped propel Trump back to the White House, and his administration has continued to make enforcement a central part of its agenda. But congressional Republicans will be competing not only for voters who remain firmly behind the president, but also for independents whose views on ICE increasingly differ from those of the Republican base.

With control of Congress at stake, the political question may be less about whether voters support immigration enforcement and more about how far they believe that enforcement should go.

text:
Greetings, readers. It’s been a bit since my last post. I’ve been fighting off a bug, but also trying to finish up some bigger projects, including my forthcoming book and new editions of both Rise of the Warrior Cop and The Cadaver King and the Country Dentist.

I’m also finishing up a long series on the outrageous conviction, death sentence, 30-year-imprisonment, exoneration, and now possible re-prosecution of Chris Duncan in Louisiana. It’s a story I’ve been covering on and off for 20 years.

Duncan was convicted in 1998 of the rape and murder of 2-year-old Haley Oliveaux, his girlfriend’s daughter. He was convicted primarily due to the testimony of Steven Hayne and Michael West, two forensic charlatans that were the subject of our Cadaver King book. In 2009, I broke the story about a video West took of his exam of Oliveaux in which he clearly uses a dental mold of Duncan’s teeth to create the bite marks on the little girl’s body that were later used to convict Duncan.

It took another 15 years, but Duncan was finally exonerated and released from prison last year. But the current district attorney in Monroe, Louisiana has, inexplicably, vowed to prosecute Duncan again.

The series should be ready soon. It’s horrific and heartbreaking story.

But in the meantime, here’s a 12-minute overview of Duncan’s case I worked on with NBC News that aired last week:

Reader mail

In my last post, I argued that if they retake Congress, Democrats should create a cause of action to sue not just federal law enforcement officials, but also policymakers like Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, and other political appointees who make decisions and give orders that predictable result in clear violations of Constitutional rights. Somewhat more controversially, I also suggested that Congress make that cause of action retroactive. One reader was not happy with me.

I was very disturbed to read your latest piece advocating for retroactively punitive laws. The concept is abhorrent, and an affront to the very idea of a "nation of laws." While the actions and policies of the people you would have these laws target are equally abhorrent, that in no way excuses entertaining the possibility of what you are suggesting.

Pointing out that the SCOTUS has created precedents that may allow such retroactively punitive laws is hypocritical, at best. The SCOTUS has quite a history of embracing concepts that are not only unconstitutional, but just plain wrong as well. This is clearly one of those cases.

I have been reading your material since your early days writing The Agitator blog, and I have long admired your tenacious pursuit of justice, both in specific cases, and as a concept in general. You have been an outstanding journalistic leader in pointing out bad laws and the bad SCOTUS precedents that have allowed those laws to exist. To see you now advocating for bad laws, and citing bad SCOTUS precedent as supporting the idea, is extremely disappointing.

I completely agree with your premise that any policy-makers who clearly flout the laws and the Constitution should not be allowed to get away with their actions and not suffer serious repercussions. But enacting retroactively punitive laws is not a legitimate way to go about making that happen.

I think eliminating the possibility of future policy-makers getting off scot-free is the best we can hope for, and a great many very significant changes will have to be made for that to become a reality.

The Constitution prohibits ex post fact laws because it’s inherently unfair and unjust to impose criminal penalties on someone for something that wasn’t a crime at the time they did it. You can’t require people to abide by laws that aren’t yet laws.

What Miller, Homan, Trump, immigration officers, and countless others in this administration are doing is entirely different. They are knowingly and willingly violating the Constitutional rights of undocumented immigrants, legal residents, and U.S. citizens under existing law. They are not only violating the Constitution on a near-daily basis, they’re inflicting real harm and injury on people, up to and including death. These are crimes. They were crimes at the time they were committed, they’re crimes now, and they’ll be crimes tomorrow.

The problem is that there is no reliable way to hold the people who committed these crimes accountable. Trump has promised a blanket pardon for criminal liability, and the Supreme Court has made it all but impossible to sue any member of the federal government. All three branches of government have completely abdicated their duty to uphold the Constitutional rights of the people Trump is targeting. I am not suggesting that Congress create new crimes. I’m suggesting they create a remedy for the people harmed by this administration’s previous and ongoing actions that are already illegal.

It’s true that I also think such a law should not exclude punitive damages. Just to be clear, punitive damages are monetary damages that go beyond compensation for pain and suffering, lost income, and generally making a victim whole. The entire reason we allow for punitive damages in civil law is to serve as a deterrent for especially harmful, egregious, and reckless behavior. I can’t imagine behavior more harmful, egregious, and reckless than the violence, terror, and death that this administration has rained down on Minneapolis, Chicago, Los Angeles, Memphis, and immigrant communities all over the country. And I can’t imagine any two groups of people more in need of a deterrent to such behavior than (1) the armed federal law enforcement officers who are entrusted with the power to detain, arrest, injure, and kill, and (2) the most powerful people who make policy decisions for the most powerful government in the world.

What I’m reading:

A Trump-affiliated oil company called “Greenland Energy” — which was formed just last year — is apparently setting up to start drilling and extracting oil in Greenland, despite the fact that Greenland has explicitly denied them permission to do so. This is theft. It is arguably an invasion. And it’s the sort of thing that would bring military strikes if another country attempted it on U.S. soil. And just to underscore our current surreal reality, there’s this: “Greenland Energy has retained Phil McGraw, better known as Dr. Phil, a prominent right-wing former chatshow host who served on Trump’s religious freedom commission, to make a documentary series that will ‘capture the mission of these modern-day wildcatters.’”

How the right’s narrative of a “censorship-industrial complex” took root and went viral. Relatedly: How right-wing chud Mike Benz got journalists like Matt Taibbi on board with the censorship narrative. Benz, by the way, is also a big reason why Elon Musk dissolved USAID.

Speaking of which, the latest insane conspiracy theory on the far right is that rap music is a massive USAID-funded conspiracy to undermine U.S. culture. Or something like that.

As they were deciding on the legality of Paramount’s takeovers of CBS and Time Warner, Trump-appointed FCC commissioners Brendan Carr and Olivia Trusty were accepting lavish gifts from Paramount executives.

Trump has recently lost at the Supreme Court on his insane and arbitrary tariffs, his attempt to repeal birthright citizenship, and his transparently dishonest attempt to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook. He’s now trying to do all three of those things, anyway.

The Trump administration thinks the attorney general — and at the moment that also means the president — should get to decide which federal prisoners serve time in which prisons. Here’s why that is a bad idea.

So far this fiscal year, 99.96 precent of the refugees the administration has taken have been white people from South Africa. The others — three in total — were from Afghanistan. And Trump later revoked their status.

Meanwhile, the roundup of Haitians who came here legally, lived here legally, and have been assets to their communities . . . has begun.

Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill is refusing to pay people who are eligible for compensation under a fund started by the legislature to pay the wrongly convicted. Most of these were not close calls. They were clear, DNA-backed exonerations of people who spent decades in prison. Murrill has fought 22 out of 23 claims. Her predecessor Jeff Landry (who is now the governor and, weirdly, also Trump’s “special envoy to Greenland”) also fought nearly every claim. Incidentally, Murrill is also supporting the Monroe DA in his fight to re-try Chris Duncan.

The president has been coating everything he sees in gold as he extracts billions from his office for himself and his family. Meanwhile, the service members fighting his war don’t have toothpaste, hot water, or working toilets.

The “concession” that senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn got from Trump in exchange for their cowardly votes to confirm Todd Blanche will still forgive any tax liability Trump or his family currently have (which is estimated to be hundreds of millions of dollars). It also immunizes him, his family, and his companies from any accountability for financial crimes they may have committed up until earlier this year. The good news is that it seems unlikely that a future administration would be required to abide by it. The bad news is that we now have Attorney General Todd Blanche.

But be sure to watch to the end, when he talks about how a far-right, Christian nationalist, anti-Muslim, Trump-endorsed Republican candidate for Congress just lost by 20 points in a Michigan primary.

“That’s great!” you’re thinking. “What’s the problem?” Well, he lost to a guy named Tom Smith, who raised less than $2,000, and who actually tried to drop out of the race.

text:
LOWELL — Immigration and Customs Enforcement says it plans to take custody of a Lowell man accused of raping a child and seek his deportation, calling him a “criminal illegal alien from Nigeria.”

ICE said in a statement to The Sun that it lodged a detainer request on July 22 with the Lowell Police Department for 54‑year‑old Patrick Akpore Nsumei, following his arrest on charges including aggravated rape of a child, rape of a child with force, and indecent assault and battery on a child under 14.

A detainer asks local authorities to hold a person for ICE or notify the agency before release.

Nsumei is a teacher at Brighton High School, which is part of Boston Public Schools. He is listed on the school’s website as a science teacher. District officials have not responded to media inquiries as to his status.

The alleged victim in this case is not connected to Boston Public Schools and is not a student in the district.

Nsumei is currently being held without bail at the Billerica House of Correction after he was found a danger to the public during a dangerousness hearing in Lowell District Court on July 31.

“Under President Trump and Secretary (Markwayne) Mullin, criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S.,” the statement concluded. “ICE is working diligently to remove these violent, dangerous offenders from our communities.”

During the dangerousness hearing, prosecutor Sheehan McCarthy detailed allegations that the victim disclosed to the Lowell Police on June 27, describing what she called the “repeated rape” of the child between 2017 and 2021.

“He’s a danger to the community at large as he’s a demonstrated pedophile and rapist,” McCarthy told Judge John Coffey during the hearing.

Nsumei’s attorney, Thomas Mixon, countered that there is not a “scintilla of physical evidence to corroborate” the allegations.

“If you believe what the Commonwealth argued here … I respectfully suggest there would be physical evidence,” Mixon told Coffey. “A pediatrician more than likely would have picked up on these types of things.”

Coffey ultimately sided with prosecutors, ordering Nsumei held without bail for up to 120 days in the Billerica House of Correction as the case moves forward in court. If the case is still pending when that period expires, the Middlesex District Attorney’s Office can seek another dangerousness hearing to continue holding him.

The top charge in the indictment, aggravated rape of a child, includes a potential sentence of life in prison with a possibility of parole after 10 years.

Nsumei — who court records show has an address on Butman Street in Lowell — is currently scheduled to return to court for a probable cause hearing on Sept. 1.

text:
U.S. Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-CA-37) is calling on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to provide immediate medical care to a constituent she says has been denied treatment after being shot by ICE officers last year.

Speaking on the House floor, Kamlager-Dove urged ICE to provide urgent care for Carlitos Ricardo Parias, describing him as a father, husband and community volunteer who was recognized by his local city council for his service.

According to Kamlager-Dove, Parias was shot near his elbow by ICE during an encounter in October. She said he received initial treatment at a hospital but has not received proper medical care since being transferred to the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in December.

The congresswoman said she visited Parias in late May and found his condition had worsened. She said his hand had turned purple, his fingers had become atrophied, and he was suffering from headaches and persistent nerve pain.

“I am worried that he may have a bone infection, and that his arm could be amputated,” said Kamlager-Dove during her remarks.

Kamlager-Dove said Parias’ case highlights broader concerns about medical care at the Adelanto detention facility. She noted that a federal judge recently ordered sweeping changes to improve conditions for detainees.

“It is time for ICE to comply with this judge’s orders and end this cruelty at Adelanto and nationwide,” she said.

ICE has not publicly responded to the allegations raised during Kamlager-Dove’s House floor speech. The congresswoman urged the agency to provide Parias with immediate medical treatment while implementing the court-ordered reforms at the Adelanto facility.

text:
Arrests after anti-immigration and counter protests

Ten people have been arrested after anti-immigration and counter protesters marched through Bristol city centre.

Demonstrations began in Queen's Square at about 10:30 BST before stopping on Bristol Bridge and outside Bridewell Police Station, and finally ending at the Cenotaph.

Avon and Somerset Police said an estimated 150 anti-immigration protesters and 300 counter protesters took part, with Supt Karen Corrigan said adding there were "pockets of disorder, especially at the Cenotaph".

Six of those arrested were suspected of concealing their identity at a protest, an offence covered by new rules which enable police to create a designated zone where face coverings are not allowed.

Other alleged offences included assault by beating, assaulting an emergency worker, obstructing a public highway, intentionally causing harassment, alarm or distress, using threatening or abusive words/behaviour, and acting in a disorderly way.

The protest caused disruption in the city centre, with key routes closed to traffic and couples on their way to get married at Bristol Registry Office seen having to walk through police lines.

Police said some disorder occurred between officers and counter-protesters, and then between the two groups with counter-protesters attempting to breach the police lines.

"When one group tries to push through this clear boundary, officers must take proportionate actions and force to maintain the line and prevent disorder," Corrigan said.

About 300 police officers were deployed to the protest, with Avon and Somerset Police supported by officers from 10 different forces.

Corrigan said: "I would like to thank and recognise the officers on the ground and those behind the scenes who enabled today's protest and counter-protest.

"Protest policing is challenging, dynamic and ever-changing; one action or word can take a peaceful protest closer to disorder and our officers must quickly and effectively adapt and change."

She also said the force used loud speakers to inform people of the new face coverings law and gave them opportunity to remove them before taking action.

"This is a challenging law to carry out, especially when faced with such huge numbers of attendees, but the initial feedback from my bronze commanders is we were seeing fewer people with face coverings than we may have in previous protests," she added.

title: Many immigrants face deportation without a lawyer at their side in court. This program tries to help
authors: Rebecca Santana, immigration policy, ICE operations, employment-based immigration, apnews.com, rebecca-santana
description:
“Folks go into immigration court not knowing what’s happening.
And when there’s an attorney present,” Chohan said, “it’s just so helpful.” Immigrants aren’t provided an attorney but legal help makes a difference Unlike criminal court, there is no guaranteed lawyer in immigration courts.
After immigrants file into the courtroom for their hearings, Judge Susan Phan introduces Chohan and describes the services her organization offers.
A changing immigration court system Chohan has witnessed the upheaval in the immigration courts during Republican President Donald Trump’s second term.
She was in the court hallways last summer when ICE officers waited to arrest immigrants after their hearings.
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — Lawyer Kamalpreet Chohan ran her finger down a list of 57 names of people scheduled to appear during a morning of hearings at the immigration court in California’s capital and pointed out one glaring absence.

“None of these folks are represented,” she said.

Chohan is the coordinator of a program that sends volunteer lawyers to immigration courts to assist people without representation and help them navigate the complicated legal system where the stakes are a future in America or deportation.

Appearing without a lawyer opens up even greater risk under the second Trump administration, with the courts playing a key role in its mass deportation agenda. Courts are increasingly denying asylum, deportation officers have arrested immigrants in court hallways, the administration has packed courtrooms to cut backlogs and reduced lead time on hearings, prompting people to miss them.

Data shows that legal representation can be vital to winning in court but many immigrants, unable to pay for a private lawyer or find a pro bono one, navigate the system without an attorney at their side.

“Folks go into immigration court not knowing what’s happening. They come out not knowing what’s happening. And when there’s an attorney present,” Chohan said, “it’s just so helpful.”

Immigrants aren’t provided an attorney but legal help makes a difference

Unlike criminal court, there is no guaranteed lawyer in immigration courts.

Immigrants have to hire one at a cost of thousands of dollars or hope to get represented by one of the nonprofit organizations assisting low-income immigrants. But waitlists with those organizations are long, and many parts of the country just do not have that many immigration attorneys.

Of the roughly 3.2 million pending deportation cases currently in U.S. immigration courts, people in 52% of those cases do not have a lawyer, according to an analysis of immigration court data by the Vera Institute of Justice, a think tank.

A Congressional Research Service study from 2024 found that only 19% of people who did not have a lawyer won asylum or another avenue to stay in the United States. Among those who did have a lawyer, 47% were successful.

“Having an attorney is just super critical to be able to navigate the system successfully,” said Adriel Orozco of the advocacy group American Immigration Council.

Chohan said she frequently runs into people who have been scammed by lawyers or people posing as lawyers who take their money but do nothing for their case.

“I will give him a list of attorneys who are free and we have vetted,” she told one man who said he was scammed. “They have long waitlists but he should still ask.”

Speaking later to The Associated Press, the man described how he left Guatemala after being threatened by gangs and came to the U.S. in 2024 seeking asylum. Ever since, he said he has done everything that has been asked of him while he tries to make ends meet, occasionally painting houses. He spent $4,500 on a lawyer who in the end did nothing to help him, he said.

“He turned out to be a scammer,” said the man, who did not want to be identified for fear of endangering his case. He is worried about what comes next in court after being warned by the judge that he could be deported. “I don’t know what I’m going to do,” he said.

A nonstop day of consulting with clients, shuttling back and forth into court

Outside the Sacramento building where the court is housed is a long line of immigrants waiting for appointments with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which is in the same building. Volunteers with a local anti-ICE resistance group stand ready to help.

Upstairs, two immigration judges are on the bench. One hears the in-depth individual cases of immigrants who are pursuing their claim of asylum.

The other judge has the master calendar docket, where dozens of immigrants will appear in brief hearings geared at making sure their case is ready to go to the next step.

Signs taped to the wall remind people not to videotape or record inside the court complex. A security guard makes sure no one loiters in the hallways. Most people clutch stacks of papers documenting their cases.

After immigrants file into the courtroom for their hearings, Judge Susan Phan introduces Chohan and describes the services her organization offers.

“You are not required to meet with her but it is a rare opportunity that we have someone volunteering their time,” Phan said before launching into the day’s work.

The need for a detailed asylum application

Chohan, who works with the California Immigration Project, starts each hearing in the courtroom. She has a clipboard to take notes, extra copies of forms and a crate of books for restless children attending court with their parents. She spends the bulk of her time in the waiting room, talking to immigrants after their hearings and scanning their documents to flesh out what else they need.

Speaking to one young man from Mexico, she asks to see his asylum application, noting that the judge had pointed out that it was not that detailed.

“Sometimes judges can deny a claim if there isn’t enough detail,” she said through one of the organization’s volunteer translators.

The organization frequently has clinics to help immigrants fill out their asylum application. Chohan said she will alert him to the next one.

Another woman holding a stack of documents is there with her son and wanted to make sure her children could come with her if she is deported. Chohan also briefed her on what to expect at her upcoming asylum hearing and said the organization will send her an asylum filing guide.

Chohan highlighted places on forms where people need to give answers or answer in more detail. It’s OK to write “none” but she advises them to not leave boxes blank.

Everything submitted in Spanish must be accompanied by a translation into English that must be done by a person, not an automatic online translator. Copies of every single page of a passport must be submitted. Documents must be sent in two weeks before the applicant’s hearing so the judge can review them.

Over and over, Chohan reminds immigrants to download their receipt showing they paid the $102 asylum application fee so they can submit it to the court.

Chohan said a lot of these procedures and forms are discussed in court but it is happening so fast and immigrants are listening through a translator that they do not always understand what is happening.

“A lot of times when they go into court, they’re just happy that they’re out of court and they’re not being arrested,” she said.

A changing immigration court system

Chohan has witnessed the upheaval in the immigration courts during Republican President Donald Trump’s second term.

She was in the court hallways last summer when ICE officers waited to arrest immigrants after their hearings. Earlier this summer she watched as the administration started holding “mega masters,” hearings with dozens of respondents at a time that are meant to clear a backlog but have created chaos.

Chohan said there are not enough pro bono lawyers in the Sacramento area to help everyone who needs one so the “Attorney of the Day” program is often the next best thing. She believes everyone should have access to a lawyer.

Until that day, she said, the program “helps bridge that gap.”

text:
About 1,400 unaccompanied immigrant children across New York, including approximately 700 upstate, are at risk of losing legal services and court representation after the Trump administration terminated a contract with Acacia Center for Justice and its nationwide network of nearly 100 legal service providers.

The children are represented by nine New York organizations in Acacia's network, including the Empire Justice Center, which has an office in Albany. Kristin Brown, the organization's president and CEO, said staff are now scrambling to determine what comes next for its clients after the July 31 expiration of its contract.

"It's heartbreaking knowing that so many children will be cut loose to fend for themselves in a legal process that was designed to be navigated with a trained attorney," Brown said, adding, "So many of the children we work with are dealing with complex trauma and they need an attorney who not only knows the law, but also knows how to communicate information in a way that is understandable and does not cause harm or confusion."

Immigration attorneys help immigrants pursue legal protections such as asylum or Special Immigrant Juvenile Status and guide them through often complex immigration proceedings, which are civil administrative cases in which individuals are not entitled to a government-provided attorney.

Children who enter the U.S. without a parent or legal guardian are legally classified as unaccompanied minors and transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which places them in shelters or foster homes until they turn 18 or are reunited with a sponsor. Since December 2023, Acacia has held the prime contract for the Office of Refugee Resettlement's Unaccompanied Children Program, which falls under the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

The termination followed months of negotiations between Acacia and HHS over the withholding of more than $65 million in congressionally appropriated funds for legal services that have already been provided. HHS said it withheld the money due to a "contract dispute."

"The government has demanded that Acacia hand over privileged client information, information that would violate attorney-client privilege, as a condition of getting paid," a spokesperson for Acacia said during a virtual press conference last Friday.

On Tuesday, HHS awarded a new contract to Houston-based Burke Law Group, though these services do not begin until Aug. 15 and will only apply to those currently in the Office of Refugee Resettlement's care. That leaves children who have already been released to caregivers or sponsors - many of whom are still navigating immigration proceedings - without a clear path to continued legal representation.

Several immigrant rights advocates have raised concerns about the selection, over one of the firm's founders' ties to the Trump administration.

Brown said Empire Justice Center expects to transfer several cases to Burke Law Group while determining how to handle its remaining clients.

A spokesperson within the HHS Administration for Children and Families said the department's Office of Mission Acquisition Solutions continues to pursue all avenues to provide legal services for unaccompanied immigrant children. This includes using the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants to provide legal representation to minors in Office of Refugee Resettlement care.

The national organization

Kids in Need of Defense also represented unaccompanied immigrant children in New York. But in June, the organization announced that

it would end its role as an Acacia subcontractor because of the federal government's overdue payments.

"The attacks on federally funded legal service providers and the ongoing delay in payments to these organizations, as well as the unreasonable demand for sensitive data, fail to reflect the vital role attorneys play in protecting unaccompanied children and upholding the rule of law," KIND president Wendy Young said at the time.

At the beginning of 2026, HHS reported an average of over 2,000 children in the Office of Refugee Resettlement's care, though that number has declined since April. In recent years, the majority of unaccompanied minors came from Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, according to federal data.

There were previously several nonprofits across New York that held contracts with the Office of Refugee Resettlement, but New York Focus reported in May that many of those contracts have been terminated in recent months.

In Washington, lawmakers have long called to uphold legal protections for unaccompanied children. In December, U.S. Rep. Daniel S. Goldman, a Democrat whose district includes lower Manhattan and much of the Brooklyn waterfront, introduced an amendment to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to repeal or amend provisions that specifically undermined protections and heightened dangers for unaccompanied children. Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-Brooklyn, supported the measure, though it never reached the House floor for a vote.

text:
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested 1,226 illegal immigrants in Georgia during an enhanced enforcement operation targeting individuals with criminal histories, according to the agency. Dubbed “Operation Safe Community–Atlanta,” the operation resulted in the arrest of 720 people who had either been convicted of or charged with crimes in the US, ICE said. The agency said the arrests involved offences including sex crimes, crimes against children, aggravated assault, drug offences, burglary, weapons violations and driving under the influence.

ICE: Operation targeted criminal offenders

“Our officers did what they do best: They arrested and removed dangerous criminal offenders from American communities,” ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Acting Assistant Director Patricia Hyde said in a statement. ICE said all 1,226 individuals arrested during the operation were in violation of US immigration law, while more than 700 also had criminal histories in the country.

Trucking company among locations targeted

ICE officers also arrested five illegal immigrants at the address of a trucking company that the agency said was known for employing illegal immigrants. Among those arrested was Fabian Pineda-Garcia, a Mexican national with prior convictions for conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute at least 500 grams of methamphetamine and driving while intoxicated, according to ICE. The agency also identified Jose Felix Amaya-Pineda, from El Salvador, who had prior arrests for domestic battery/family violence, cruelty to children, disorderly conduct and driving while intoxicated. Other arrests included Elena Marin, a Romanian national with prior arrests for theft by deception and petit larceny, and Armando Loma-Cristo, a Mexican national previously arrested on allegations including DUI, supplying alcohol to underage people, child endangerment and driving without a valid licence, ICE said.

ICE steps up enforcement

The Georgia operation comes as the Trump administration continues to intensify immigration enforcement across the US. ICE has been carrying out targeted operations against illegal immigrants with criminal records, with the agency saying the efforts are aimed at removing dangerous offenders from American communities.

description:
Latest death in ICE custody Additional deaths have since occurred of migrants in ICE detention since June 4.
His death is the 20th death in ICE custody this year.
That’s a 140% increase in deaths in ICE custody from the same time the previous year.
“People are dying in ICE custody at the highest rate in many years, even after accounting for the surge in detention,” said Brian Root, senior technology and human rights adviser at Human Rights Watch.

text:
HARLINGEN, Texas (Border Report) — Since President Donald Trump took office for his second term, at least 52 people have died in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody, according to a new report.

The report, “Dying in Detention,” released Thursday by the nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights, says “the mortality rate of deaths in ICE custody is at its highest level in over a decade and has more than doubled since Trump’s second term began. The rate is nearly four times that of the Biden administration, and more than two and a half times as high as that of the first Trump administration.”

The report was compiled using data from Jan. 20, 2025 through June 4.

Latest death in ICE custody

Additional deaths have since occurred of migrants in ICE detention since June 4.

This includes the June 19 death of a 63-year-old Mexican national at the Webb County Detention Center in Laredo, Texas. ICE reported on Wednesday that Felix Alcorta-Rodriguez “was found unresponsive” at the detention center, and medical emergency services were called and lifesaving measures were employed. He was taken to a local hospital where he pronounced dead. His death is the 20th death in ICE custody this year.

Alcorta had been taken into custody by ICE officials on June 16 after being released by the Webb County Jail. He had been initially arrested on May 9 due to an outstanding warrant for failure to appear in court for a Feb. 5, 2018, driving while intoxicated arrest, ICE officials said.

Report criticizes ‘aggressive’ detention campaign

The Physicians for Human Rights report says the Trump administration’s “aggressive campaign to expand immigration detention” has pushed detention facilities and staff to their limits — reaching a high of 71,000 incarcerated in January 2026.

However, the report says “the surge in deaths is much worse than what one would expect even considering the much higher number of people in detention. Deaths in ICE custody have increased at a rate disproportionate to the growth in the detained population.”

The 72-page report says there were 39 deaths reported in the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, from Jan. 20, 2025, to Jan 19, 2026. That’s a 140% increase in deaths in ICE custody from the same time the previous year.

“People are dying in ICE custody at the highest rate in many years, even after accounting for the surge in detention,” said Brian Root, senior technology and human rights adviser at Human Rights Watch. “DHS and Congress should act immediately to reduce the number of people in detention and to overhaul conditions, including by ensuring access to adequate health care in line with the United States’ human rights obligations.”

The deaths included that of a 44-year-old man from Ukraine who suffered a stroke; a 39-year-old Mexican citizen who reportedly died from a cardiac arrest that Physicians for Human Rights assessed likely arose from overwhelming septic shock; and a 32-year-old man who died in 2025 following a COVID-19 diagnosis and 12 days in isolation, the report says.

The report also criticizes the agency for not releasing enough information on the individual deaths, and says oversight of these detention facilities is hindered because of a lack of transparency.

“ICE so severely limits the information it provides to Congress, families, and the public that oversight is nearly impossible,” said Dr. Katherine Peeler, the report’s co-author, assistant professor of pediatrics at Harvard Medical School, and medical adviser at Physicians for Human Rights. “In the cases where we do have access to ICE and outside hospital records, we are seeing a breathtaking breach of the duty of care.”

ICE says one of its highest priorities is detained migrant health care and that its national detention standards require facilities to provide comprehensive medical, dental and mental health care from the moment migrants arrive at a facility and throughout their time in ICE custody.

“Many aliens may not have received recent or reliable medical treatment for existing conditions prior to entering ICE custody,” the agency says on its website. “For some individuals, this may represent their first access to comprehensive medical care.”

ICE says it is agency policy to notify the relevant parties and report the death of any detainee in a “timely, accurate and appropriate manner,” adding that it notifies next of kin, appropriate consulates, relevant DHS and ICE stakeholders, U.S. Congress and the public about each detainee death.

Sandra Sanchez can be reached at SSanchez@BorderReport.com.

title: Weaponized Migration: When Mobility Becomes a Weapon of War – NAOC
authors: Jaiden Ahuja, Author Jaiden Ahuja, Author Ryan Krueger, Author Jacqueline Hicks
description:
As an unconventional non-military tactic, weaponized migration has emerged as a new form of hybrid warfare.
Embedding Weaponized Migration within Ongoing Crises NATO’s concern for weaponized migration can first be attributed to a growing tendency of adversaries including Russia to worsen ongoing conflicts by intentionally displacing civilians.
The effects are clear: By embedding weaponized migration within larger, ongoing conflicts, adversaries are able to reduce their opponent’s response capacity.
Firstly, through intelligence sharing, NATO can work to conduct risk assessments that identify potential migration routes that may be vulnerable to weaponized migration.
Evidently, NATO’s efforts to curb weaponized migration must increasingly evolve, so that adversaries cease viewing migrants as weapons of war.
text:
Lured by Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s promise of a future in the European Union (EU), thousands of migrants would travel to Belarus leading up to the fall of 2021. Many arrived with no return ticket or personal belongings. However, by November, their experience would turn out far different than they had expected. As thousands of migrants sat in front of barbed wire fences erected at the Polish border in freezing conditions, their role as tools to sow chaos within the EU became apparent as asylum systems were placed under pressure. Overwhelmed by the influx of migration at their borders, Poland, Latvia, and Lithuania responded by declaring states of emergency. Yet, in inciting chaos at their borders and challenging the territorial integrity of these three NATO Members, Belarus did not need to rely on sophisticated technology or its military force. Instead, it leveraged migration, transforming human desperation into a potent weapon.

As an unconventional non-military tactic, weaponized migration has emerged as a new form of hybrid warfare. According to security studies expert Kelly Greenhill, weaponized migration consists of the “manipulation of population movements as strategic means to political and military ends”. By manipulating the flow of migration, nefarious actors can destabilize countries, incite chaos, instrumentalize vulnerable individuals, and fuel social divisions over immigration while operating below the threshold of war. Ultimately, weaponized migration is emerging as a grave security concern for which the NATO alliance must be prepared. In balancing its security interests with humanitarian protection, NATO must equip itself to adequately respond to the manipulation of migration flows reappearing in conflict.

Embedding Weaponized Migration within Ongoing Crises

NATO’s concern for weaponized migration can first be attributed to a growing tendency of adversaries including Russia to worsen ongoing conflicts by intentionally displacing civilians. During the Syrian Civil War, NATO Supreme Commander Philip Breedlove claimed that “together, Russia and the Assad regime [were] deliberately weaponizing migration from Syria, in an attempt to overwhelm European[s].” Indeed, by targeting civilian infrastructure with airstrikes, Putin and Assad conspired to expel refugees towards Europe. Similarly, following its invasion of Ukraine, Russia has continued to employ weaponized migration, bombing civilian infrastructure in an effort to generate waves of migrants bound for neighbouring NATO member states.

The effects are clear: By embedding weaponized migration within larger, ongoing conflicts, adversaries are able to reduce their opponent’s response capacity. Military resources are diverted, border infrastructure is stretched, and sustained pressure is created along critical frontiers. Furthermore, the impacts are not merely operational but political. As Greenhill notes, the victims of weaponized migration are overwhelmingly liberal democracies. Thus, by targeting civilians and driving migration towards these countries, adversaries can exploit rising anti-immigration sentiment by causing a divide as to how governments should respond and diminishing trust in state institutions when the response is deemed inadequate. Consequently, weaponized migration constitutes a serious concern for NATO given its capacity to exhaust material resources, social cohesion, and public trust.

Manufacturing Migration Crises

Beyond weaponized migration being used as a singular tactic embedded with larger conflict, NATO should be concerned by how adversaries are manipulating migration flows to manufacture independent crises as instruments of coercion. In 2021, Belarus simplified its visa process, attracting migrants and refugees from Iraq, Syria, and Afghanistan with the promise of entry into Western Europe. Upon their arrival, the Lukashenko government transported them to its borders with three neighbouring NATO countries (Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland) in an attempt to destabilize the area. Poland’s deployment of 20,000 security personnel to its border with Belarus and construction of a 400km border wall that cost 350 million euros illustrate how migration crises – independent of larger conflicts – can be manufactured to disorient the security forces of NATO states.

Yet, as weaponized migration is used to manufacture pressure towards European NATO members, it is also no stranger across the Atlantic. In November of 2021, Nicaragua dropped its visa requirements for Cubans, granting them the ability to travel upwards to the United States by land as opposed to sea. However, the timing of such a measure was not coincidental; Nicaraguan President Ortega introduced the new visa policy directly after the United States cited unfair elections in Nicaragua and imposed sanctions against him. The direct and mass spur of Cuban migration towards the United States indicates that weaponized migration is becoming a routine tool employed to give the user leverage against regional adversaries. The instrumentalization of migrants by Belarus and Nicaragua raises major concerns for NATO as such crises can be manufactured by simple policy changes. By loosening visa requirements and attracting desperate individuals, weaponized migration has proven to be an emerging threat given how inexpensively and rapidly it can be employed.

Navigating Migration Threats

NATO’s response to this new hybrid threat must balance security considerations with humanitarian ones. For instance, the responses of Poland, Latvia, and Lithuania to Belarus’ manufactured migration crises were motivated by fear, panic, and repression. The hasty use of tear gas, water cannons, and physical violence points to unpreparedness and unease as soldiers trained to handle enemy combatants responded to huge civilian flows. Yet, NATO must not forget that migrants used as weapons are human beings. To improve its response, NATO must balance security and humanitarian challenges by offering both preventive and operational support.

Firstly, through intelligence sharing, NATO can work to conduct risk assessments that identify potential migration routes that may be vulnerable to weaponized migration. By predicting where and when migration is likely to be directed by adversaries, NATO can ensure a measured as opposed to hasty or panicked response. Beyond sustained readiness, NATO must continue to emphasize the importance of deployment mobility. As established at the 2016 Warsaw Summit, a key principle of national resilience is the “ability to deal effectively with the uncontrolled movement of people”. Under its Resilience Committee, NATO’s Civil Protection Group addresses ways to ensure this principle is upheld. The creation of this group suggests that NATO is taking the threat of weaponized migration more seriously. Furthermore, by complementing intelligence sharing and readiness with the operational means to absorb, distribute, and respond to irregular migration flows, alliance members can fulfil their obligation under Article 3 of the North Atlantic Treaty to develop the capacity to resist an armed attack through effective help and mutual aid. While weaponized migration may not itself constitute an armed attack, its potential to be embedded within larger conflicts that cross such a threshold illustrates the need for collective operational assistance.

Migration is a process that can enable cultural and economic interconnectivity. But when artificially controlled to manufacture crises at the expense of the vulnerable, it becomes a threat to peace and security. By compounding migration pressures onto existing conflicts and manufacturing entirely new crises, countries continue to use civilian movement as an instrument of coercion. However, by developing risk assessments, intelligence sharing, and operational readiness while ensuring the rights of migrants and refugees are upheld, NATO can respond to weaponized migration in a way that balances security and humanitarian concerns.

Political scientist Mark Leonard warned of governments seeking to turn migrants “into bullets”. Unfortunately, this is increasingly coming to fruition. Evidently, NATO’s efforts to curb weaponized migration must increasingly evolve, so that adversaries cease viewing migrants as weapons of war.

title: Two Trump cases that will impact Colorado | Jimmy Sengenberger - Denver Gazette
description:
Two incoming U.S. Supreme Court cases illustrate why.
Circuit Court of Appeals ruled 2-1 against the Trump administration’s deportation policy of denying bond outright to illegal immigrants “seeking admission” to the country pending removal proceedings.
The New Orleans-based Fifth Circuit and St. Louis-based Eighth Circuit have sided with Trump — a split the U.S. Supreme Court will almost certainly have to resolve.

A 2006 Supreme Court decision created the “Purcell principle,” discouraging last-minute changes to voting rules.
text:
Perhaps no presidential administration has spent more time in court — defending its policies against lawsuit after lawsuit — than President Trump’s.

Two incoming U.S. Supreme Court cases illustrate why. Both will ultimately reach Colorado.

Last week, a panel of the San Francisco-based Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled 2-1 against the Trump administration’s deportation policy of denying bond outright to illegal immigrants “seeking admission” to the country pending removal proceedings.

The ruling doesn’t bind Colorado, which sits in the 10th Circuit, but it marks the fifth appeals court to reject the policy. The New Orleans-based Fifth Circuit and St. Louis-based Eighth Circuit have sided with Trump — a split the U.S. Supreme Court will almost certainly have to resolve. The Trump administration has already asked the justices to take the case.

Previous presidential administrations let noncitizens without criminal records seek bond. Trump ended that. But as the Fifth Circuit majority noted, the fact that “prior administrations decided to use less than their full enforcement authority” doesn’t mean they lacked authority for more.

In dissent, Ninth Circuit Judge Carlos Bea found the text and intent of Congress’s 1996 immigration overhaul — which redefined who counts as an “applicant for admission” — on the administration’s side.

Let’s be real: Sneaking across the border or overstaying a visa doesn’t make someone lawfully present. They still need to be granted admission.

Imagine a teenager caught after sneaking into Elitch’s. “I’m not seeking admission,” the teen protests. “I’m already inside!”

Except jumping the fence doesn’t mean you’ve been admitted. You needed a ticket. Without it, you’re outta here.

As former Denver ICE Field Director John Fabbricatore told me in April, “We’ve seen too many times where an alien will bond out and disappear again.” He cited an estimated 1.7 million final removal orders never carried out — including for criminal aliens.

District courts have split, too. In Colorado, the only federal judge to uphold the policy is Chief Judge Daniel Domenico — who is now, pending a confirmation by the full U.S. Senate, headed to the 10th Circuit.

In one key ruling, Domenico wrote that “admission” means “the lawful entry of [an] alien into the United States after inspection and authorization by an immigration officer” and “not simply physical entry into the country.” The petitioner hadn’t been lawfully admitted, making him an “applicant for admission under the law.”

Domenico acknowledged most district courts have found the policy improper, adding that there are “legitimate arguments on both sides.” But his conclusions reflect his “best understanding of the law,” and he’s “duty-bound” to follow that reasoning, whether district court rulings have “reached inconsistent outcomes” or not.

At his Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin pressed Domenico on being an “outlier” on these cases. Domenico gave the same answer he’d put in written opinions and noted that he’d “in fact ruled against the federal government’s position and granted petitions a number of times.”

The Senate should confirm Domenico posthaste.

The Supreme Court ought to side with the administration here.

On the second case — where the consequences land squarely on Colorado — it shouldn’t for the same overarching reason: the law points the other way.

The Centennial State has run universal mail elections since 2013. Every active registered voter receives a ballot by mail. Trump’s March 31 executive order would put the Postal Service and Department of Homeland Security between Coloradans and their ballots, requiring the feds to screen state voter rolls against federal eligibility lists.

On practical grounds, it’s untenable. Federal databases are less accurate and slower to correct than Colorado’s. Worse, it would force Colorado to break its own universal mail ballot law.

Two-thirds of Colorado voters cast their ballots by drop box, not mail. The postal choke point here isn’t how Coloradans return a ballot but whether they receive one as they’re entitled.

Ironically, Pew Research found Trump’s mail-in margin rose nine points between 2020 and 2024 while his in-person margin fell five points. He’s moving to restrict the voting method that helped reelect him.

The Justice Department is now 0 for 20 in lawsuits seeking state voter rolls. Twelve of those judges were Republican appointees. Eight of them are Trump’s own.

The latest came Monday from Judge Philip Brimmer, a George W. Bush appointee to Colorado’s federal district court, who found the DOJ provided no sufficient justification or valid purpose for demanding the rolls — and isn’t entitled to unredacted information anyway. He dismissed the case with prejudice.

The Supreme Court is currently being asked only whether to lift an injunction while litigation continues, not whether the order is lawful. If the administration wins, a case on the merits could follow. The administration should lose.

A 2006 Supreme Court decision created the “Purcell principle,” discouraging last-minute changes to voting rules. If courts mustn’t change the rules this close to an election, a president certainly can’t rewrite them by fiat, with fewer than 100 days until Nov. 3.

More importantly, Article I of the U.S. Constitution assigns state legislatures the authority to set the “Times, Places and Manner” of federal elections, letting Congress alone “make or alter such Regulations.”

The president isn’t included. Trump can’t rewrite state election rules with the stroke of his pen. Full stop.

These aren’t partisan distinctions. The law is what matters. Defending a president’s authority when the law grants it means nothing if we go silent when it doesn’t.

title: Is ICE using much force? New poll shows big public opinion shift - USA Today
description:
Months of immigration enforcement controversies have taken their toll, and new polling shows it could be a problem for Republicans heading into the midterms.
