text:
Months of immigration enforcement controversies have taken their toll, and new polling shows it could be a problem for Republicans heading into the midterms.

About eight in 10 independent voters say U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has used too much force in its nationwide operations, according to a poll from YouGov, which sampled 1,000 voters in late July. It's a striking increase from 2025, when polls showed independents more divided on the issue.

The poll, commissioned by the Vera Institute of Justice, a nonprofit working to end mass incarceration, was conducted shortly after ICE agents shot and killed two immigrants during traffic stops in Maine and Texas over the span of six days in July.

An earlier YouGov poll, which was conducted before the two shootings, found that most independents – 62% – believe ICE has gone too far. Other polls from YouGov, AP-NORC and The Civic Health and Institutions Project found that only a fraction of independent voters support ICE's handling of immigration enforcement.

The data comes months ahead of the midterms, as Republicans are seeking to hold onto a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress. Several races are expected to be close and could be decided by independent voters – a group whose support has grown increasingly vital in recent elections.

The Department of Homeland Security in an emailed statement cited June polling data showing 80% of Americans support "deporting immigrants who are here illegally and have committed crimes.” The statement urged cities to cooperate with ICE and praised the work of immigration officers.

Immigration was one of the top issues that led Republicans to win the presidency and gain full control of Congress in 2024, amid mounting frustrations over the Biden administration's handling of the U.S. southern border. But high-profile enforcement raids and multiple deadly shootings over the last year have eroded support for a central part of President Donald Trump's immigration agenda, political scientists and strategists said.

But not all of the president's actions on immigration are as unpopular as ICE's interior enforcement. The plunging number of border crossings into the U.S. is considered a success among at least half of all Americans, including independents, polls show. And Republicans overall maintain a sizable advantage on which party voters believe would do a better job at handling border security.

But with the midterms less than three months away, any uptick in disfavor for ICE among independents could spell trouble for Republicans seeking to win over voters from the center, experts said.

“This is a big vulnerability,” said Matthew Grossman, a political scientist and professor of public policy at Michigan State University. “An issue that [Republicans] had in previous elections is now working to their disadvantage.”

In a statement, National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson Mike Marinella said GOP candidates running in the midterms will continue to embrace Trump's record on immigration and draw a contrast with the Biden administration.

“President Trump secured the border and is finally enforcing the law after four years of Biden-Harris chaos that let fentanyl and criminals pour into this country and cost American lives in every district," he said. "Democrats spent four years defending open borders and calling it compassion while Americans paid the price. Republicans will keep drawing that contrast in every district, because voters haven’t forgotten what lawlessness looks like.”

'The public mood has changed'

Trump was elected with a promise to carry out the largest deportation operation in U.S. history. On the campaign trail, his supporters held signs that read “MASS DEPORTATION NOW!” And in a 2024 interview with Time magazine, Trump said he wanted to deport “probably 15 million and maybe as many as 20 million” people.

Polls conducted in the months before the 2024 election saw Trump leading Biden by roughly 20 points on immigration and border security. Some polls found that for most voters, immigration was their top issue.

But controversies have eroded that support.

Surges of federal agents into cities such as Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis fueled mass protests, lawsuits and widespread claims of harassment and racial profiling. In January, public outrage spiked following the fatal shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good by immigration agents in Minnesota.

In the aftermath, immigration authorities sought to keep a lower profile, moving away from the highly visible raids that drew intense scrutiny. Republicans, meanwhile, talked less about mass deportations and more about targeted enforcement going after criminals, as well as the low number of border crossings.

But protests and backlash reignited again in July after ICE agents in Texas and Maine shot and killed two men in less than a week. And while immigration authorities have largely halted their high-profile raids, ICE detentions have surged.

A poll from The Associated Press and NORC conducted after the shootings found that 39% of adults approved of Trump’s performance on immigration, down from 49% at the start of his term.

According to the same poll, three in 10 adults approve of the way ICE is enforcing immigration laws. Among independents, 18% approved of ICE’s actions.

“This has consequences for the campaigns,” said Kyle Kondik, a political analyst who has written several books on U.S. elections. “Some of the messaging that Republicans thought was effective in 2024 on immigration may not be anymore because the public mood has changed.”

Immigration remains a deeply partisan issue

Polls show that views on immigration largely fall along party lines, as has been the trend for more than a decade, experts said.

Less than two out of 10 Republicans say ICE has used excessive force, and most either said the agency has used “about the right amount of force” or “not enough,” according to the YouGov poll conducted in July. Democrats, meanwhile, remain firmly opposed to the immigration enforcement operations underway, with nine out of 10 saying ICE has gone too far.

In primary races across the U.S., immigration was one of the central issues in campaign speeches and advertisements, especially in areas that saw large amounts of enforcement actions.

Some Democratic candidates who won their party’s nomination have called for ICE to be abolished, including progressives in Michigan, Illinois and New Jersey.

On the Republican side, many primary candidates leaned into immigration, spending tens of millions on advertisements that mention or were solely focused on the issue, according to data from the firm AdImpact. Those in areas that have seen controversial ICE actions have walked a tightrope, criticizing some tactics while supporting popular immigration-related initiatives like enhanced border security.

It’s largely proved successful. On Aug. 4, a slate of Trump-backed Republican candidates who support the administration’s immigration enforcement efforts won the GOP nomination in Washington state, Kansas and Michigan.

But, as analysts note, candidates often appeal to their party's hardline or most vocal factions in primaries before later tempering their messages.

“They’re speaking to a different electorate in the primary than they are in the general,” Grossman said.

What does this mean for the midterms?

It’s unclear how much of an impact immigration will have on the November elections, analysts said. A lot can happen by the time voters head to the polls. And in each district, voters’ priorities are different.

The YouGov poll conducted in late June and early July found that cost of living, inflation and the economy were the top issues for voters – not immigration, which ranked below healthcare policy and international military conflicts. Recent polling from Pew Research Center and Marquette Law School showed similar results.

But like immigration, public support for Trump’s handling of the economy and the Iran war has waned, giving Republican candidates limited options for a positive messaging strategy heading into November, analysts said.

Experts suspect Republican candidates will focus their messaging on their opponents in coming months.

“Their current positive sign, as [Republicans] see it, is Democrats are nominating more extreme candidates,” Grossman said, speaking about the wave of progressives who’ve won Democratic primaries across the country. “That might mean more negative campaigns going into the fall.”

GOP leadership has already begun employing this tactic.

During an Aug. 5 speech focused on the economy and how his policies have lowered costs for Americans, Trump repeatedly turned to the progressive wing of the Democratic Party.

“These people are dangerous and, frankly, lunatics,” Trump told the crowd at a Las Vegas casino. “They’re crazy, and we can’t let them get into office.”

Christopher Cann is a national reporter for USA TODAY. Contact him by email at ccann@usatoday.com.

In June, the Supreme Court held that the 14th Amendment extends citizenship to children born to those parents.

text:
“That includes, for example, alien enemies,” Miller said.

Trump’s first birthright citizenship order would have denied automatic citizenship to children born in the United States to parents who were either in the country illegally or present only temporarily. In June, the Supreme Court held that the 14th Amendment extends citizenship to children born to those parents.

Chief Justice John Roberts rooted that ruling in the citizenship clause’s “broad reach and narrow exceptions.” He wrote that the clause begins with territory, requiring a person to be “born … in the United States,” and ends with sovereign power, requiring that person to be “subject to the jurisdiction” of the U.S.

The chief justice said a child born in the U.S. and subject to U.S. law “was made an American citizen.” The established exceptions, he said, were “carefully defined,” covering children of foreign ministers and members of 19th-century Indian tribes over whom the U.S. had ceded part of its territorial jurisdiction.

Trump’s new citizenship order attempts to operate in those narrower areas. It directs agencies to deny citizenship to children born to certain foreign government officials, employees of international organizations with immunity, individuals designated as “alien enemies,” and parents who used commercial arrangements to travel to the U.S. to give birth.

South Texas College of Law professor Josh Blackman said Trump is trying to identify questions that Barbara did not conclusively answer.

“I think he’s trying to find vulnerabilities in the chief’s opinion,” Blackman told the Washington Examiner.

The American Samoa factor could offer courts a lesser explored legal territory

One provision of the orders specifically highlights people born in a U.S. territory or territorial waters where citizenship is not conferred by federal statute. Blackman said that language appears to point to American Samoa and could give the administration a distinct test case that has little to do with the broad rule settled in Barbara.

People born in American Samoa are generally U.S. nationals rather than U.S. citizens at birth, unlike people born in Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and the Northern Mariana Islands. Blackman said American Samoa appears to be the only current example contemplated by Trump’s provision.

“It’s an issue not from Barbara, but something called the Insular Cases,” Blackman said, “Which is that people in these various territories are not citizens by birth. … So he’s testing the Insular Cases there as well.”

The executive order could face litigation on that point more readily than other provisions, Blackman said. A pregnant woman from American Samoa could have a direct injury and standing to sue, although her case would not necessarily answer the separate questions involving foreign officials, alleged birth tourists, or designated alien enemies.

Blackman said the administration may otherwise confront more difficult standing problems. States could argue that denying citizenship to people born within their borders would reduce federal funding tied to population, but the Supreme Court did not resolve that theory in Barbara because the earlier litigation involved individual plaintiffs.

Testing what Trump v. Barbara did not decide

Blackman said Trump’s strategy is to force lower courts and, eventually, the Supreme Court to address each category separately rather than reconsider the broad question decided in Barbara.

The alien enemy provision is one example. The majority’s historical account noted the common-law understanding that children born after enemies “possess” a U.S. “castle or fort” were not born under U.S. allegiance. Trump’s order seeks to apply that principle to people designated as alien enemies under federal law, including members of certain foreign terrorist organizations.

“Barbara didn’t decide the status of alien enemies, so that’s not controlled,” Blackman said.

Finding an individual challenger to that provision could prove difficult because few people would likely come forward to identify themselves in court as members of a designated terrorist group. A business that arranges birth tourism travel could also attempt to sue, Blackman said, although its standing would present its own questions.

The provision involving children of ambassadors and other foreign officials rests on a more established footing, Blackman said. Roberts explained that foreign ministers are treated differently because of a legal “fiction of extraterritoriality,” under which diplomats remain, in some respects, under their home country’s sovereignty.

“The children of ambassadors, I think Barbara said they’re not citizens,” Blackman said, although he added that defining which other foreign government employees qualify may be more difficult.

Roberts also drew a sharp contrast between diplomats and ordinary foreign visitors. Citing an early Supreme Court case, he wrote that private foreign nationals who enter the country for “business or caprice” are “amenable to the jurisdiction of the country.” The majority found no similar foreign sovereignty concern for parents who are in the U.S. illegally or temporarily.

“[What] Trump’s doing is basically forcing the Supreme Court to look at each item separately, not just writ large and entire orders,” Blackman said.

Administration aims to stop birth tourism before it happens

The order’s treatment of birth tourism may pose the most difficult constitutional question, and by all considerations appears to be an area where options to crack down are more limited.

Miller explained that the administration sees birth tourism as a form of visa fraud rather than ordinary travel by a pregnant woman. “Birth tourism is, by definition, a fraud on the American system,” he said.

“If you’re telling a consular officer you’re here as a tourist, but your true purpose and intent is to go to a baby mill, give birth, and try to mint an American citizen while you’re here, then you’re committing a fraud against the American government,” Miller said. “And by definition that visa can, and should, and will now be denied.”

Trump’s separate order targeting birth tourism directs the State Department and Department of Homeland Security to develop regulations and guidance aimed at preventing foreign visitors from using temporary visas to give birth in the U.S.

Former acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement Director Jonathan Fahey said the visa-focused component could have practical effects even if the broader citizenship restrictions face litigation.

“If you’re already pregnant and your purpose is to have a child, to have it become a citizen, that would become visa fraud if you lied about that,” Fahey said Friday on Fox News’s Varney & Co. He also argued that stricter enforcement could deter organizations that profit from arranging birth-tourism travel because prospective clients may no longer expect citizenship for their children.

“I think that’s going to be really effective on the deterrence aspect,” Fahey said. “Overall, this is going to be very effective, even if it doesn’t end up being upheld in the courts.”

But Blackman said the administration’s attempt to deny citizenship to children of birth tourists is “the hardest one” legally because “there’s no obvious historical reason why they’re excluded.”

The White House appears to be arguing that fraud used to obtain entry into the U.S. creates an “extraterritorial fiction” that places those children outside the birthright citizenship rule, Blackman said. Yet Roberts’s opinion is a potential obstacle, because it said “temporary visitors remained subject” to U.S. jurisdiction while here and that their children are citizens at birth.

More legal analysts critical of the orders say they stretch limited exceptions under the current law beyond recognition. Tianna Mays, legal director at Democracy Defenders Action, told NBC News that the administration lost “the central constitutional argument” in Barbara and is now trying to stretch narrow exceptions “until it swallows the whole 14th Amendment.”

TRUMP SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDERS TO CURB BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP AND ‘BIRTH TOURISM’

Lucas Guttentag, a law professor at Stanford and Yale, told the outlet that the birth tourism directive largely restates powers the government already has under immigration law.

Trump’s new orders are narrower than the policy the court rejected, but they are also designed to test a subset of legal boundaries that Roberts described in his ruling without clearly defining himself.

text:
Federal immigration officers arrested more than 1,200 illegal immigrants in the Atlanta, Georgia area, including 720 who DHS said had been convicted of or charged with crimes.

Speaking on “Fox & Friends,” Marcos Charles, executive associate director of ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations, said the sweep took violent criminals — including sex offenders and child abusers — off the streets.

“We arrested over 1,200 aliens, illegal aliens, out in the Atlanta, Georgia area. More than half of those people had criminal histories,” Charles said.

“We’re talking about sex crimes, assault and battery, some with DUI convictions, domestic violence. These individuals needed to be taken off the street, not only because they’re criminals, but because they are here illegally in the United States,” he added.

The Department of Homeland Security announced online that the sweep, called “Operation Safe Community – Atlanta,” focused on criminal illegal immigrants.

“Every day, the men and women of ICE ERO were out in the streets across the nation, enforcing the immigration laws as set forth by Congress. So we’re keeping the community safe. We’re [going to] be traveling all over the United States doing the same thing,” Charles said.

In July, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recorded approximately 51,000 immigration arrests, which ICE said was its highest monthly total ever, surpassing the 43,000 arrests recorded in June.

Charles said agents have adapted their tactics because of protests and what he described as efforts to interfere with arrests, including changes to how they track individuals in the country illegally.

“What we’ve done is we’ve adapted to that, not only with additional training, but we’ve adapted our methodology on how we conduct these enforcement efforts and our arrest methods,” he said.

Among those arrested, DHS identified a Mexican national with prior convictions for “conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute at least 500 grams of methamphetamine and driving while intoxicated.”

DHS also identified an illegal immigrant from El Salvador with prior arrests for “domestic battery/family violence, cruelty to children, disorderly conduct and driving while intoxicated.”

The operation comes months after DHS reported an 8,000% increase in death threats against ICE officers. Some progressive lawmakers have also called for abolishing ICE over concerns about the agency’s enforcement operations.

text:
WASHINGTON — Congress should expand the nation’s legal immigration pathways before attempting to strengthen immigration enforcement, arguing that decades of inaction have left workers and employers without viable legal options, Cato Institute Director of Immigration Studies David J. Bier wrote in a commentary published Tuesday.

The op-ed argued that the immigration debate fixates on post-entry amnesty versus deportation, neglecting the lack of available legal pathways. Bier contends that this approach ignores the core issue of enabling legal immigration in the first place.

Bier explained that Congress has not significantly updated America’s legal immigration system in nearly four decades. The most recent reforms, initiated by the Reagan administration, made it possible for seasonal workers to enter legally with work permits through the H-2A visa program.

“It took until the late George W. Bush administration for all the relevant agencies to get the system working properly,” Bier noted. “But today, it finally provides an orderly and legal path for over 315,000 workers per year.”

The program largely solved the problem of illegal immigration in the seasonal agriculture industry. Bier emphasized that today, however, 86% of undocumented workers “aren’t in agriculture at all.”

“They’re in construction, hospitality, restaurants, delivery and other non-seasonal sectors, which have no path to hire anyone legally,” Bier continued. “If Congress is serious about illegal immigration, it needs to create a system that both immigrants and employers can use.”

The first step, Bier proposed, would be for Congress to create a work visa that allows employers to hire “vetted legal immigrants” for year-round jobs. These workers, primarily low-skilled, would not have access to welfare.

This change, according to the article, would also allow immigration enforcement to practically “take care of itself.” With a legal pathway available, fewer workers would need to enter illegally, and employers would have a legal way to hire them.

“President Donald Trump himself has publicly recognized the economic problem with deporting illegal immigrants in agriculture, hospitality and other sectors,” Bier stated. “If enforcing our current system can’t get the enthusiastic backing of the most hardcore enforcer in American history, it’s time to fix it.”

According to Bier, low-skilled American workers will also benefit from increased access to legal immigration. More legal immigrant workers would allow businesses to expand, fill needed positions, create managerial positions and expand opportunities for specialized workers.

“Visit a restaurant and see this complementarity play out,” Bier wrote. “Many Americans can see directly how immigrants increase our productivity by caring for our children or ailing elderly parents.”

The analysis proposed that highly skilled immigrant workers would need their own set of reforms for the nation to reap the full benefits of legal immigration. According to Bier, the H-1B lottery that these workers rely on for visas rejects over 60% of applicants, preventing them from starting businesses and entering high-level positions.

Bier also argued that the country loses potential economic growth when highly skilled immigrants are unable to remain in the United States long term. Acquiring a green card is “torturously slow,” and some applicants will have to wait decades to receive one.

“High-skilled legal immigrants massively reduce federal, state and local deficits by a combined $11.7 trillion over the last 30 years,” Bier pointed out. “Their inventions and ingenuity hold the potential to increase the productivity, and therefore the wages and living standards, of all workers in the economy.”

Bier ultimately calls for a legal immigration system that reliably responds to the nation’s economic demands, enabling immigrant workers of all skill levels to enter the country and encourage market growth.

text:
About 1,400 unaccompanied immigrant children across New York, including approximately 700 upstate, are at risk of losing legal services and court representation after the Trump administration terminated a contract with Acacia Center for Justice and its nationwide network of nearly 100 legal service providers.

The children are represented by nine New York organizations in Acacia’s network, including the Empire Justice Center, which has an office in Albany. Kristin Brown, the organization’s president and CEO, said staff are now scrambling to determine what comes next for its clients after the July 31 expiration of its contract.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“It’s heartbreaking knowing that so many children will be cut loose to fend for themselves in a legal process that was designed to be navigated with a trained attorney,” Brown said, adding, “So many of the children we work with are dealing with complex trauma and they need an attorney who not only knows the law, but also knows how to communicate information in a way that is understandable and does not cause harm or confusion.”

Immigration attorneys help immigrants pursue legal protections such as asylum or Special Immigrant Juvenile Status and guide them through often complex immigration proceedings, which are civil administrative cases in which individuals are not entitled to a government-provided attorney.

Children who enter the U.S. without a parent or legal guardian are legally classified as unaccompanied minors and transferred to the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which places them in shelters or foster homes until they turn 18 or are reunited with a sponsor. Since December 2023, Acacia has held the prime contract for the Office of Refugee Resettlement’s Unaccompanied Children Program, which falls under the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

The termination followed months of negotiations between Acacia and HHS over the withholding of more than $65 million in congressionally appropriated funds for legal services that have already been provided. HHS said it withheld the money due to a “contract dispute.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“The government has demanded that Acacia hand over privileged client information, information that would violate attorney-client privilege, as a condition of getting paid,” a spokesperson for Acacia said during a virtual press conference last Friday.

On Tuesday, HHS awarded a new contract to Houston-based Burke Law Group, though these services do not begin until Aug. 15 and will only apply to those currently in the Office of Refugee Resettlement’s care. That leaves children who have already been released to caregivers or sponsors — many of whom are still navigating immigration proceedings — without a clear path to continued legal representation.

Several immigrant rights advocates have raised concerns about the selection, over one of the firm’s founders’ ties to the Trump administration.

Brown said Empire Justice Center expects to transfer several cases to Burke Law Group while determining how to handle its remaining clients.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

A spokesperson within the HHS Administration for Children and Families said the department’s Office of Mission Acquisition Solutions continues to pursue all avenues to provide legal services for unaccompanied immigrant children. This includes using the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants to provide legal representation to minors in Office of Refugee Resettlement care.

The national organization Kids in Need of Defense also represented unaccompanied immigrant children in New York. But in June, the organization announced that it would end its role as an Acacia subcontractor because of the federal government’s overdue payments.

“The attacks on federally funded legal service providers and the ongoing delay in payments to these organizations, as well as the unreasonable demand for sensitive data, fail to reflect the vital role attorneys play in protecting unaccompanied children and upholding the rule of law,” KIND president Wendy Young said at the time.

At the beginning of 2026, HHS reported an average of over 2,000 children in the Office of Refugee Resettlement’s care, though that number has declined since April. In recent years, the majority of unaccompanied minors came from Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, according to federal data.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

There were previously several nonprofits across New York that held contracts with the Office of Refugee Resettlement, but New York Focus reported in May that many of those contracts have been terminated in recent months.

In Washington, lawmakers have long called to uphold legal protections for unaccompanied children. In December, U.S. Rep. Daniel S. Goldman, a Democrat whose district includes lower Manhattan and much of the Brooklyn waterfront, introduced an amendment to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to repeal or amend provisions that specifically undermined protections and heightened dangers for unaccompanied children. Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-Brooklyn, supported the measure, though it never reached the House floor for a vote.

text:
President Trump’s second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship tees up another legal battle over the meaning of the 14th Amendment.

The administration designed Trump’s new orders more narrowly in hopes of withstanding legal scrutiny, but the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and Democratic-led states are already signaling they’ll bring them to the courts.

Here’s what to watch as legal scrutiny heats up.

What the justices have said about ‘birth tourism’

Trump’s announcement focuses on “birth tourists,” referring to people who come to the country to give birth so their child can get automatic U.S. citizenship.

“Wealthy people are building businesses around birthright citizenship. That’s not the way it was supposed to work. It’s a disgrace,” Trump said in the Oval Office as he signed the new orders.

It’s been an ever-present topic in the legal battle.

When the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 against Trump’s original attempt on birthright citizenship, Chief Justice John Roberts emphasized that the Constitution’s citizenship guarantee is broad. People who come to the U.S. for business or pleasure are not exempted, he noted.

“To the contrary, they were subject to that jurisdiction for as long as they remained here—and any children born to them were American citizens under the Fourteenth Amendment,” Roberts wrote for the majority.

The chief justice didn’t use the term birth tourists back in June. But the dissenters made the implications clear.

“As interpreted by the Court today, the Fourteenth Amendment confers citizenship on virtually everyone who happens to be born in this country, including the children of ‘birth tourists,’” Justice Samuel Alito noted.

Justice Clarence Thomas similarly said the decision had recognized “a constitutional right to citizenship for the children of all foreign birth tourists and illegal aliens.”

Roberts didn’t disagree. But he has long rebuffed the notion that it should’ve affected the outcome.

“You do agree that that has no impact on the legal analysis before us?” he pressed the Trump administration at oral arguments earlier this year.

Trump’s directive is more than birthright citizenship

Trump’s new crackdown on “birth tourists” does include a direct attempt to restrict their child’s citizenship. It would block it if someone committed “fraudulent activity” or made a “commercial transaction” in coming to the U.S. specifically to give birth, including the use of a surrogate.

But the president’s directive includes a second, legally distinct piece.

The president is claiming his authority to further restrain the already illegal practice of birth tourism under a 74-year-old federal statute that senior officials in his administration have often cited to justify their intense immigration crackdown.

The rationale centers on Section 215(a) of the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), which governs the travel of noncitizens in and out of the country. It grants the president the power to make “reasonable rules, regulations and orders” regarding who can enter and exit the U.S. and under what conditions.

White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller hailed it as a “very rarely used” mechanism that is “probably one of the strongest laws” in the federal code.

The administration has argued that foreign nationals who misrepresent their reason for coming to the U.S., specifically by concealing plans to give birth, are violating that rule and should have their visa applications denied or revoked.

“If you’re telling a consular officer you’re here as a tourist, but your true purpose and intent is to go to a baby mill, give birth, and try to mint an American citizen while you’re here, then you’re committing a fraud against the American government, and by definition, that visa can and should and will be now denied,” Miller said in the Oval Office.

Whether the president can lawfully restrict tourist visas on this basis is a separate question from the Supreme Court’s decision in June, setting up a new battle over how far the government can go in policing fraud.

And Trump’s allies believe it will succeed this time around.

“What we’re doing is taking legally validated means clearly within our disposal and targeting them square on to this birth tourism industry,” said White House Staff Secretary Will Scharf, a former federal prosecutor who was also one of Trump’s personal defense lawyers.

“There’s absolutely nothing in here that runs afoul of any of the Supreme Court’s opinions on the subject,” he added.

Trump has latched onto a separate opinion authored by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, one of his own appointees, who had partially sided with the president back in June.

Kavanaugh voted that Trump wasn’t violating the 14th Amendment, only a federal law. He hinted that Congress could always amend that law to include new exceptions, however.

“Congress in 1940 and 1952 enacted a statute, §1401(a), that at the time and since has always been understood to authorize only the four Wong Kim Ark exceptions,” Kavanaugh wrote. “If Congress amends §1401(a) or otherwise enacts a statute creating new exceptions along the lines of the Executive Order for children born to foreign citizens unlawfully or temporarily in the country, such a statute, as I see it, would pass constitutional muster.”

But now, Trump is making another attempt without Congress.

Trump’s focus on ‘alien enemies,’ foreign governments

Trump’s policy would restrict birthright citizenship for two other categories beyond birth tourists: the children of “foreign government employees” and “alien enemies.”

The administration is expected to argue both fall within the long-recognized exemptions to the 14th Amendment, teeing up judges to test the boundaries.

On both sides of the debate, legal experts agree the Constitution doesn’t provide automatic citizenship to the children of foreign sovereigns, ambassadors and diplomats.

While parts of Trump’s announcement simply restate that consensus, his order ensures citizenship doesn’t get extended to the babies of anyone working for a foreign embassy or consulate who is a national of that country, anyone employed by a foreign government in an official capacity and anyone who has legal immunity as part of their role with an international organization, such as the United Nations or World Bank.

Domestic immigration agencies already hold that citizenship should not be automatically conferred on children of certain foreign diplomatic officers because they are not “subject to the jurisdiction” of the U.S. by reason of their immunity.

To justify their opposition, conservatives also often argue that noncitizens lack allegiance to the U.S. and are beholden to their home countries.

The final category covered by Trump’s order is the children of an “alien enemy.”

He’s defined that to include members of foreign terrorist organizations and other designations.

The Supreme Court has long recognized an exception in the 14th Amendment for when occupying forces or enemy invaders have children during a hostile occupation on American soil.

Now, Trump argues there is an “invasion” at the southern border. He formally declared an invasion on Inauguration Day and has leveraged it to unlock expansive legal authorities as part of his immigration crackdown.

Potential lawsuits on the horizon

No lawsuits challenging the two new orders have been filed yet, but it didn’t take long for civil rights groups and Democratic attorneys general to signal plans to do so.

Cody Wolfsy, the deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, vowed in a statement shortly after the orders became public on Thursday that any new attempt by the administration to “rewrite” birthright citizenship would “meet the same fate as the last one.”

“The Supreme Court already decided this issue: Birthright citizenship is guaranteed by the Constitution,” said Wolfsy, who served as lead counsel for the plaintiffs in the Supreme Court case. “No additional executive order can change the meaning of the Constitution.”

Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford (D) said his office “immediately” began reviewing the directives.

“If these executive orders run afoul of the law, we will see the president in court and, just like last time, we will win,” he warned. “While President Trump believes he can dismantle the Constitution with a wave of his hand, our nation’s founders established the rule of law.”

“We will teach him that lesson as many times as he needs to learn it.”

description:

text:
That’s an important distinction. The former accepts the constitutional order by working within it to challenge it. The latter rejects the constitutional order entirely.

Their actions align with the strategy of Nazi political theorist Carl Schmitt, whose writings seem lately to have captivated leaders on the American right. Schmitt opposed liberal democracy, in which the state enables individuals to determine their own fate.

Instead, he argued that true democracy erases individual self-determination by making the mass of people one with the state and exercising their will through state power. That uniformity requires getting rid of opposition. Schmitt theorized that politics is simply about dividing people into friends and enemies and using the power of the state to crush enemies. As J.D. Vance described Schmitt’s ideas in 2024: “There’s no law, there’s just power.”

Much of Schmitt’s philosophy centered around the idea that the power of a nation that is based in a constitution and the rule of law belongs to the man who can exploit emergencies that create exceptions to the constitutional order, enabling him to exercise power without regard to the law. Trump—who almost certainly has not read Schmitt himself—asserted this view in August 2025 to justify deploying troops to American cities.

“I have the right to do anything I want to do,” he said. “I’m the president of the United States. If I think our country’s in danger — and it is in danger in the cities — I can do it.”

Although the Republicans have control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate—meaning Trump should be able to get his agenda passed according to the normal constitutional order—since retaking office he has operated under emergency powers.

Back in April, Ben Diamond of Lawfare noted that Trump is on track to issue six and a half times more emergency orders in his second term than any other president this century issued during his entire term. That number, Diamond suggests, is probably an underestimate because many of Trump’s orders do not include the keyword “emergency” and so fly under the radar.

Trump’s imposition of a new round of tariffs on products from more than 60 countries, making up 99.4% of trade with the U.S., is a flashing red light.

In April 2025, the administration imposed high tariff rates on countries around the world, claiming legal authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), which permits the president to respond quickly to economic threats during a national emergency. On the same day he announced the tariffs, Trump declared “that foreign trade and economic practices have created a national emergency.”

When the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs as unconstitutional, Trump immediately announced he would find “other alternatives… to replace the ones that the court incorrectly rejected. We have alternatives,” he said. “Great alternatives.” The administration turned to Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the president to impose tariffs in the case of an international financial emergency.

Those tariffs are limited to 150 days. When that deadline hit on July 24, Trump announced he was imposing tariffs under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose tariffs on countries that are using forced labor. A senior administration official told reporters that the tariffs were not an attempt to recreate the previous system and that dealing with the issue of forced labor “is something that President Trump has been focused on…for many years.”

But law professor Barry Appleton, who co-directs New York Law School’s Center for International Law, said: “The 301s allow a permanent tariff without going to Congress to settle the dispute. That’s what all of this is about. The president doesn’t want to knock on the front door of Congress, so he’s trying every side door and every unlatched window to get in.”

Let’s be very clear here: tariffs are revenue measures, and the U.S. Constitution explicitly gives the power to raise revenue to Congress, not the president. Article 1, Section 8, reads: “The Congress shall have Power To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare of the United States; but all Duties, Imposes and Excises shall be uniform throughout the United States.”

This clause was almost the whole game. Control over the nation’s money, sometimes called the power of the purse, was central to the Framers’ concept of republican government. The American Revolution took shape over the determination of colonists to have a say in how their government raised money, a right first articulated in the Magna Carta that in 1215 established the principle that the king did not enjoy absolute power. A key check on him was that he could not pass revenue measures without the consent of the governed.

And so the Framers put it in the Constitution.

But control over the revenue was not quite the whole game. The Framers were also crystal clear that the people must have control over the decision to go to war. They did not trust that much power in the hands of one man and wanted to make sure the American people would have robust debates about the value of the money and lives lost in combat.

So determined were they for the American people to have those debates that they wrote into the Constitution that Congress had the sole power “[t]o declare War” and “[t]o raise and support Armies, but no Appropriation of Money to that Use shall be for a longer Term than two Years.”

Here, too, Trump has used the idea of an emergency to sidestep Congress’s authority by insisting the threat from Iran was “imminent” even though his own advisors testified that Iran did not, in fact, have the capacity to build a nuclear weapon in less than ten years.

Under the 1973 War Powers Act, a president has the authority to respond to an “imminent threat” without congressional approval so long as he notifies Congress in writing within 48 hours. Then the president has 60 days either to withdraw U.S. forces from their engagement or to get Congress to authorize the military action.

Trump launched U.S. attacks on Iran on February 28. He notified Congress on March 2. Sixty days from March 2 was May 1. When that deadline arrived, Trump sent letters to House speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and Senate president pro tempore Chuck Grassley (R-IA), officially the leader of the Senate if the vice president is not present, to inform them that so far as the White House is concerned, “the hostilities that began on February 28… terminated” on April 7, when Trump ordered a two-week ceasefire.

Although hostilities and a U.S. blockade of Iran continued, the administration maintained the ceasefire was in place until July 10, when Trump notified Congress for a second time that the nation was engaging in military action in Iran. The administration maintains that this second notification is for a new military engagement and thus restarts the clock under the War Powers Act. Legal analysts say this interpretation has no basis in law, legislative history, or practice.

The Trump administration is claiming the powers of Congress both to tax and to declare war, key powers the Framers established the American people’s right, through their representatives, to control.

When Senator Angus King (I-ME) and five Democratic lawmakers who sit on committees responsible for national parks and resources wrote in June to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to oppose “in the strongest terms” Trump’s proposed triumphal arch, they pointed out that there are many different laws the construction would break. “Most fundamentally,” though, they wrote, the arch falls within an area called Area I that Congress established in the 1986 Commemorative Works Act.

In that law, Congress specified that any commemorative work within Area I requires Congress to pass a law authorizing the memorial. The lawmakers wrote to Burgum: “Because the site is in Area I, the Act requires a second, separate approval, under which Congress must enact a law ratifying the Area I location within 150 days of the Secretary’s notification, following a determination that the subject is of preeminent historical and lasting significance to the United States. Congress has enacted no such laws. Analysis we requested from the Congressional Research Service in January reached the same conclusion: absent these authorizations, construction of an arch in Memorial Circle would not comport with the Commemorative Works Act. Since 1986, every memorial placed on federal land in the capital under the Act, more than forty in all, has come to Congress first…. The Arch’s sponsor has sought no act at all.”

“If the Administration believes the semiquincentennial warrants a permanent commemorative work in the capital,” they wrote, “the path is open and well worn; it runs through Congress, as it has for every memorial since the Continental Congress approved the first, an equestrian statue of George Washington, in 1783.”

Back in October 2025, when officials first acknowledged to reporters that Trump was planning to build an arch, a reporter asked Trump about a model of an arch that was sitting on the desk in the Oval Office.

“It’s an Arch,” he said. “Take a look.”

When a reporter asked who the arch was for, Trump pointed at himself and said: “Me.”

title: United Airlines Accused of Colluding With ICE to Lure Woman to Gate at Phoenix Sky ... - PYOK
description:
Gore is now accusing United Airlines of colluding with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after one of the carrier’s gate agents in Phoenix repeatedly made announcements for Patience to go to the gate where the ICE agents were lying in wait.
During bag drop, no issues had been raised by the United agents, but Patience dutifully made her way to Gate E7.
On her arrival, the United gate agent repeatedly referred to Patience’s boarding pass.
At this point, three male undercover ICE agents who weren’t wearing any visible identification or badges suddenly surrounded Patience and made it clear that she wasn’t free to go.
The detention did, however, mean that Patience missed a round of IVF treatment that she was scheduled to undergo at home.
text:
What should have been the end of a happy weekend celebrating a friend’s wedding in Arizona turned into a living nightmare when Patience Gore, a Zimbabwian national, was detained by three undercover ICE agents at the Phoenix Sky Harbor Airport (PHX) and subjected to two weeks of ‘degrading confinement’ in immigration custody before a court ordered her release.

Gore is now accusing United Airlines of colluding with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after one of the carrier’s gate agents in Phoenix repeatedly made announcements for Patience to go to the gate where the ICE agents were lying in wait.

The incident occurred late on Sunday, March 15, when Patience and her partner arrived at Phoenix Sky Harbor to fly home to Maryland after a busy weekend celebrating a friend’s wedding. They were booked on United flight UA-483 to Washington Dulles, and had checked in, dropped off their luggage, and obtained their boarding passes without any issues.

The couple then went through TSA security and waited in the departures concourse for their delayed flight to be ready to board. During this time, Patience heard a voice over the airport’s intercom system repeatedly imploring: “Passenger Patience Gore, please come to the gate.”

Patience couldn’t work out why she would be needed at the gate, as she and her partner had checked in with plenty of time to spare, and they both had their boarding passes. During bag drop, no issues had been raised by the United agents, but Patience dutifully made her way to Gate E7.

On her arrival, the United gate agent repeatedly referred to Patience’s boarding pass. At this point, three male undercover ICE agents who weren’t wearing any visible identification or badges suddenly surrounded Patience and made it clear that she wasn’t free to go.

Patience was eventually led out of the airport and transported to a detention facility in Florence, Arizona, where she was held for three days before being transferred to the Eloy Detention Center. There, she was forced to sleep on a mattress placed directly on the floor, subjected to repeated lockdowns, and denied a change of clothes or basic personal necessities, a lawsuit filed against United alleges.

She was detained for two weeks before a court ordered her release after concluding that she had been previously granted a withholding of removal and that her removal to Zimbabwe is unlikely to occur in the near future.

The detention did, however, mean that Patience missed a round of IVF treatment that she was scheduled to undergo at home. A replacement cycle did not result in pregnancy.

In a new lawsuit filed in an Arizona district court, Patience makes it clear that United is banned from communicating with law enforcement, including ICE, and, where necessary, sharing data about its passengers.

The lawsuit does, however, claim United “retained control over how it exercised its own passenger announcement authority and used that authority in a manner that created the appearance of legitimate airline business when no airline-related issue was identified.”

Patience alleges that the presence of the ICE agents at the gate, along with the repeated announcements and the fact that the gate agents quickly lost interest in Patience once they had identified her from her boarding pass, shows that she was being called to the gate solely for the purpose of her detention.

United is being sued for negligence because of the misleading use of passenger announcements and false imprisonment. Patience is requesting damages and punitive damages, with the total claim to be more than $75,000.

United Airlines did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: 'They kidnapped a hard-working kid off our streets': the gardener seized by ICE - The Guardian
description:
For me, and a lot of other people who call this small town home, Turcios’s arrest was personal.
Henoch had come to the US in 2017 via a tortuous route, and Turcios hadn’t seen him for six years.
He spoke no English, so Weigel registered him with a county language integration programme and with the local high school.
Miller called Gregory Copeland, a law school friend who had pioneered legal strategies to stop ICE deportations and had also moved to Rhinebeck.
Turcios has been shuffled between detention facilities across three states – New York, New Jersey and Louisiana – seemingly at random.
text:
Gerson Turcios didn’t recognise the men standing next to a couple of dark SUVs outside his house one July afternoon last year. He figured they were lost and approached to see if he could help. A slim 23-year-old with short dark hair and big brown eyes, Turcios had just finished work mowing lawns in the pretty town of Rhinebeck, in New York’s Hudson Valley. The men asked if he knew someone called Jimmy – he did, but Jimmy hadn’t lived in the small, white weatherboard house with Turcios, his brother and his brother’s girlfriend for a while.

The men noted Turcios’s accent and asked where he was from. Turcios didn’t answer, so one took out his phone and snapped a photograph. The next thing Turcios knew, he was in handcuffs in the back of one of the SUVs and on his way to an ICE processing centre in Newburgh, New York, then on to a detention centre.

Mass deportation has been the defining mission of Donald Trump’s second presidency. In the year since he took office, ICE – United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement – has deported nearly a quarter of a million people from inside the US (half a million including from its borders) as part of an immigration crackdown. These forceful apprehensions, which have in some cases resulted in fatal shootings of potential deportees and bystanders, have resulted in protests – and sparked international outrage. Behind the statistics, though, are stories of hope and perseverance; of young immigrants who risked everything crossing rivers and deserts to build lives, start businesses and put down roots in communities that are now fighting to keep them.

Back then, as he was shackled and led to his cell, sure he was about to be deported back to Honduras, Turcios – an immigrant who had made a terrifying journey as a teenager, fleeing violence there – had no idea that his community in Rhinebeck was already mobilising; that they would raise tens of thousands of dollars in days, galvanise support from Hollywood actors and film-makers who also called the town home, and even recruit the lawyer who essentially wrote the book on stopping ICE deportations around the nation to represent him.

I’d moved to Rhinebeck with my own family from Texas during the pandemic, drawn to the bucolic countryside and good schools. Our own daughter now walks the same high school hallways Turcios once did. For me, and a lot of other people who call this small town home, Turcios’s arrest was personal.

“Well, it’s happened,” wrote actor Griffin Dunne on Instagram. “ICE has come to my beloved Dutchess County and kidnapped a hard working kid with his own local lawn care business, and without a criminal record, off our tranquil streets.” But he added, “This is only the beginning.” Dunne, who has a home in Rhinebeck, told his followers that the community had started a war chest to defend Turcios. “Our pressure has brought about a hearing for Gerson at 11:00 tomorrow morning at Thurgood Marshall Courthouse for those who wish to show support. To my Rhinebeck neighbors, a bus will leave from Tops [grocery store] at 7:00 am.”

Six years earlier, around 9pm on a freezing December night, Turcios and three other migrants had stood by the southern banks of the Rio Grande river in Mexico, looking across into Texas as flames torched the desert brush behind them; Mexican soldiers had set it alight to flush them out.

With nowhere left to go, Turcios turned to the others. “We are right here,” he told them. “The other side is the United States.” Another boy checked that everyone was able to swim – they were – but all Gerson could think about was alligators, which had occasionally been known to inhabit the Rio Grande.

The four boys jumped into the black water together, fighting the current as it pushed them downstream. Along that stretch, near McAllen, Texas, the width of the Rio Grande ranges from 45 to 90 meters. Finally, soaking wet, they scrambled up a concrete wall on the US side. They ran through scrubland until headlights appeared behind them, then three German shepherds. A heavier boy was dragged down by the dogs as he scaled a fence; the others scattered. Turcios sprinted until three cars boxed him in and US immigration officers emerged with guns drawn. “If you keep running,” they shouted, “we’re gonna shoot your legs.” Turcios stopped, put his hands up, then fell to his knees and felt a boot between his shoulder blades as they threw him to the ground and handcuffed him. He had spent six weeks on a journey that had nearly broken him. Against all odds, he had made it across the river. And now he’d been caught.

In 2019, during the first Trump administration, an adult detained by Border Patrol crossing into the US was increasingly likely to be sent back to Mexico to wait for their immigration case to be heard. Turcios, though, was under 18, and the law dictated he be taken to refugee resettlement housing for minors. Turcios stayed at a facility in Long Island for almost a month until his brother, Henoch, and Henoch’s girlfriend, Yorleny Weigel, were allowed to pick him up and return to Weigel’s home in Rhinebeck.

Henoch had come to the US in 2017 via a tortuous route, and Turcios hadn’t seen him for six years. Their first stop was a Wendy’s fast food joint for a burger – “So big,” Turcios now recalls, “I didn’t know how to eat it.”

He would have to wait for the government to notify him of his first immigration hearing, but soon the Covid pandemic would throw the courts into chaos, with some hearings postponed indefinitely and others rescheduled then postponed again, leaving Turcios in limbo.

Weigel showed Turcios his room, then drove him across the river to a big outlet store in the city of Kingston to buy clothes. He spoke no English, so Weigel registered him with a county language integration programme and with the local high school. In the summer of 2020, ahead of the start of the school year, he was introduced to Anna Lawson, who would be one of his classmates. Lawson was in advanced Spanish and, as Covid was still forcing people to meet virtually, they spoke regularly over Zoom. “He is a really lovely, positive person,” Lawson says. “He’d often be sitting outside, talking about how much he enjoyed Rhinebeck.”

On the first day of school, Turcios was afraid he’d be arrested by the police officer who sat outside in his car for an hour each morning as kids entered the building – just under half of US state schools have police patrol on campus – but after his first day, that fear passed. “After that I wasn’t afraid. I was excited,” he says. “But I didn’t speak any English at all.” Turcios immediately hit it off with his classmates. Brendan Dougherty shared a study hall with him. “Gerson is a very sociable guy, so it wasn’t difficult to strike up a conversation with him,” Dougherty says. “And his English progressed very quickly. Each day we’d go outside and play basketball.”

Turcios finished high school in the early summer of 2022 and began working in the kitchen of a local French restaurant and, in his spare time, for a crew that did landscaping and house maintenance, and mowed lawns. One of his first clients was Jenny Friedberg, a creative director and producer who had moved up to Rhinebeck from the city during the pandemic. Turcios and the maintenance crew painted her basement in Brooklyn, and excavated 24in of bedrock under her barn in Rhinebeck. “Whatever they did, Gerson was always there,” Friedberg says. “He was the youngest of the crew, the smiliest, the most helpful, and my favourite.”

In the summer of 2025, Turcios left the restaurant and went to work full-time with the crew. At 7.30pm on 18 July 2025, Friedberg’s phone rang. It was Carlos, Turcios’s boss. Turcios had been detained by ICE, he told her, and he didn’t know what to do.

Friedberg made several calls that evening. The first was to Luciano Valdivia, a local restaurateur and president of Rhinebeck’s chamber of commerce. The next was to Amanda Miller, a local attorney. Then John Reinish, a political communications strategist she knew. Within 24 hours, they’d set up a Spotfund, an online fundraising platform, to raise money for Turcios’s legal battle. Miller called Gregory Copeland, a law school friend who had pioneered legal strategies to stop ICE deportations and had also moved to Rhinebeck.

Copeland was a nationally recognised civil rights and immigration attorney, and co-founder of the Rapid Defense Network, a non-profit providing pro bono legal support to immigrants facing deportation. He was also the subject of the documentary Guerrilla Habeas, which looked at the legal strategy it employed to stop deportations at the last moment. That strategy hinged on filing habeas corpus petitions, which empower federal judges to compel the authorities to justify detentions, a power enshrined in the constitution. Doing this forces cases out of immigration courts and into federal court, where due process can be properly considered and immigrants have a fairer shot at justice.

Miller says Copeland had experience fighting “the biggest machine there is – the federal government”. But since his move to Rhinebeck, he had stopped practising civil rights and immigration law, and had turned his attention to estate planning for clients. Still, Miller knew there was no one better to help Turcios.

“It wasn’t clear to me immediately that I would help him, but I went into triage mode, gathering information and figuring out what our options were,” Copeland says. As soon as Copeland got Turcios’s “A-Number” – the alien registration number assigned by the US Department of Homeland Security to non-citizens– he could check his status in the system. He discovered that, years earlier, Turcios had been ordered deported “in absentia” for missing a hearing. During Covid, courts repeatedly moved locations; Turcios missed a notice despite living at the same address he’d always provided.

Copeland knew it was now vital to get the Rhinebeck community to show up for him. “If you consider what the government evaluates when justifying someone’s detention, it’s whether they’re a danger to the community and a flight risk,” Copeland says. “The community is typically not going to show up for a dangerous person. And you’re less of a flight risk if there’s a strong community around you.”

It was a matter of urgency to identify where Turcios was being taken and where he was going next. Copeland says it’s not an exact science, but after working these cases as long as he had, you get a feel for it. A red flag was if he had been sent to Louisiana, a staging location for deportations – at this point, he had not. However, Turcios had been detained with his passport – another red flag. “[The government] needs two things to remove you: a travel document and a final order of removal,” Copeland says. “They need something to show who you are because in immigration court one of the first things they need to establish is that you’re not a citizen.” If an immigrant picked up by ICE doesn’t have a travel document on them, that buys their attorneys more time.

Meanwhile, Valdivia asked Leah Conklin, another resident who worked in international criminal justice reform, to get involved. Within days of Turcios’s arrest, a crack team was coming together, but time was of the essence. “One of the reasons they make arrests on Friday, I think, is because you can’t catch up,” Valdivia says, “and if you don’t know where they’re going, you don’t know how to stop it.”

Copeland was looking at the online detainee locator system, trying to get a feel for where Turcios was moving – through which processing centre; which detention centre. In New York state, if you are taken to Federal Plaza in Manhattan and then your location “goes dark”, that’s an indicator you could be bound for a deportation flight. “It’s very relevant for filing a habeas petition,” Copeland says, “because you have to file where they’re detained.” If you don’t know where your client is, you can’t file and they can be deported. “So it’s a game they’re playing – hiding the person.”

Conklin had been calling around law firms but found it impossible to get a lawyer quickly enough. On Sunday, Copeland agreed to take on Turcios’s case himself. “I had created the Rapid Defense Network because there’s a small window in which you have to do this. It’s like a death penalty case: you have to strike while the iron’s hot or you’re dead.” By that evening, with Miller’s help, Copeland had filed an emergency petition on Turcios’s behalf, seeking a stay to allow him to consult with lawyers and challenge his removal order. Conklin says that the community came together in record time.

Valdivia messaged some other Rhinebeck residents he knew could amplify Turcios’s story. He called Dunne, the actor and writer who had starred in An American Werewolf in London and After Hours, and whom Valdivia counted as a friend. He texted film-maker Andrew Jarecki, who donated, as did actor Paul Rudd, who co-owns a sweet shop in Rhinebeck and lives there with his family. Word spread. Other contributions came in from all over the US and beyond.

Dunne began posting about Turcios’s case on social media. “It was the first time I’ve ever used Instagram without kind of being embarrassed about self-promotion because I had a movie coming out,” he says. “It made sense to me for the first time. I was just struck by the inhumanity and the contagion of cruelty.”

Friedberg says that when Turcios was arrested, she had a reckoning with herself: “This sort of recognition of how we don’t often know the people that have been working for us or near us for years.” She had never asked about Turcios’s story.

Turcios spent his early childhood in the small town of Balfate on Honduras’s northern coast. His father, Juan, raised cattle. Irma, his mother, gave birth to 10 children. The disappearance of his eldest brother, Amilcar, is one of Turcios’s earliest memories. He was four when his brother went missing after travelling by boat to Roatán, a Honduran island, to seek a better life. Of the five people who made the trip, authorities recovered the bodies of three. Amilcar and the boat’s captain were never found. Turcios’s family never learned the truth; they suspect it had something to do with organised crime, but they’ve come to accept that Amilcar is dead.

While there has been a drop in violent crime in the last couple of years, historically Honduras has been one of the most dangerous countries in the world, with gangs vying for control of drugs and extortion rackets. A decade ago, it frequently topped global lists of the highest murder rates in non-war zone countries, fuelled by its position as a major transit hub for South American cocaine heading to the US.

“My mother was afraid, so she decided we should move from that place where she lost her son,” Turcios says. The family relocated to just outside the large city of San Pedro Sula and stayed there for nine years. Turcios went to school, but eventually they sold up and moved to a house in the mountains. It was beautiful, he says, but dangerous; you could never be sure which was more deadly – the criminal gangs who stole livestock, or the venomous snakes and other wildlife.

They had 10 cows to tend and a few horses, and they began constructing their own house. Laundry was done in a small stream and cooking over fire. Walking to the city took nine hours, over mountain passes; Turcios recalls jumping on his father’s shoulders to cross rivers.

By the time Turcios moved to the mountains, his brother Henoch had already migrated to the US. Henoch says he travelled from Honduras, across Mexico by train, without any money and had to beg for food. He spent three months in Monterrey, where he almost had to have his left hand amputated due to an infection. A friend helped him pay for the medication – the same friend would eventually take in Henoch in Rhinebeck. After he’d recovered enough, he hitched a ride on a train to the border town of Sonoyta, then spent 22 days walking through the southern desert into Arizona. He says he nearly died after spending weeks without eating, surviving on nothing but water.

Eventually, Turcios’s parents decided to move back to town as they wanted his younger sisters, aged eight and 10, to go to school, and to be nearer to a hospital in case they got sick. Turcios stayed in the mountains, living alone for six months so his father wouldn’t have to sell his animals, but he was an hour away by foot from the nearest house. His father gave him a gun for safety and most nights he’d lie awake, clutching it, and listening to the cries of animals in the wilderness.

After the 16-year-old son of his nearest neighbour was murdered over drugs, Turcios’s siblings decided it was time for him to leave Honduras. One day, when visiting his sister in town, he was told that the following morning a man would arrive who would help him cross into Mexico and travel to the US to join his brother. “I didn’t have a future in Honduras,” he says. “If you wanted to go to college, you had to pay a lot of money and my parents couldn’t afford it. And I knew if I went to the United States I would learn how to speak English and it would be better for me.”

Two days later he was travelling across Guatemala by bus and car, under the “care” of a coyote – a people smuggler he had paid 12,000 Honduran pesos, the equivalent of about £350 – or, as he recalls, the amount he’d received for a cow he’d sold five days earlier. Turcios had been told the back route through the mountains would keep him safe. He, his coyote and a group of other migrants moved only at night, but safety proved elusive. At a bus stop in Guatemala, armed officers boarded and ordered passengers to strip. Turcios had hidden his money in his sock, out of sight. The coyote paid the officers off and they kept moving. Hours later, another police stop. This time the driver was pulled from the van, kicked and beaten while officers held a pistol to his head. Only when the driver produced 25,000 Mexican pesos (about £1,000) did they relent.

After 16 nights in a safe house, one migrant demanded better treatment from the people smugglers and that they get moving. Three strangers dragged him outside and he never returned.

The journey took a month and a half. In early December, Turcios and his closest companion, Antonio, were roused at midnight and, together with four others, were packed into a van and dumped in desolate brush. Turcios and Antonio were from the same state in Honduras but hadn’t known each other before. The others were from different countries – El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico. “I was 17. Antonio was 28 and like my older brother,” Turcios says. “His wife and kid had moved to the US a year before and lived in Georgia, so he was trying to reunite with them.”

A guide led them through darkness for 30 minutes. By 3am they had joined 40 others alongside the Rio Grande, shivering in the winter cold. The border was not unguarded. Helicopters buzzed low, forcing them to hide in the grassland and scrub. Mexican army troops encircled them, weapons raised, setting fire to the surrounding brush to flush out the remaining migrants, most of whom fled into the night. Turcios surrendered his pesos and ran. Then, it was time to cross.

After his capture, the US Border Patrol officers took Turcios to a room with a table and two chairs. An officer accused him of being an adult; of running drugs across the border. Turcios told them he was 17, that he had never muled drugs, and that he had gone three days without sleep or food. He produced his birth certificate, which they took and never returned. A doctor arrived, checked his teeth, and confirmed his age. Then the officers stopped yelling, moved him to a cell full of boys his age or younger, and gave him two cookies and a bottle of Kool-Aid – the best meal he had eaten in weeks.

Two days later, he was given new clothes, a jacket for the cold, and told he was flying to New York. It was his first time on a plane, his first time seeing “ice fall from the sky”, as it was snowing that day in New York City. After 26 days in a Long Island shelter, showering each morning and night, and attending a little school inside the facility, he was met by Henoch and Weigel, who drove down from Rhinebeck to collect him.

Six months after Turcios was detained outside his home in Rhinebeck, the campaign to help him had shifted from emergency response to sustained pressure. On a freezing Tuesday afternoon in January, more than 100 students walked out of Rhinebeck’s middle and high schools as part of nationwide anti-ICE protests, defying district policies that required parental permission to leave campus.

My daughter, Scout, then 14, helped organise the walkout, and I watched from the edge of the park as she stood on a podium and told the crowd how ICE had taken a Rhinebeck High School alumnus who had done nothing but contribute to the community and how his detention had affected everyone.

Turcios has been shuffled between detention facilities across three states – New York, New Jersey and Louisiana – seemingly at random. Last August he was taken to the Alexandria Staging Facility in Louisiana, a factory for deportation flights. One morning he was led on to a plane bound for Honduras, but guards pulled him off just before departure after Copeland and other lawyers working on his case won a stay of removal. Over the next 48 hours, Turcios watched as 50 other migrants left the United States, before he was driven back to the detention facility.

In June Turcios had his second court hearing; unlike the first, this one he was required to attend. Dunne says he couldn’t get out of his head the picture of this boy in ankle chains, flanked by guards, looking over at his friends and supporters in the public gallery. “And when he gave us a wave it was just heartbreaking.”

It also brought up traumatic memories. Back in 1982, Dunne’s younger sister, Dominique, died after being strangled by her ex-boyfriend. “The last time I was in a courtroom was over 40 years ago, representing my sister who had been murdered,” he says. “I attended the trial every day … and every day felt like a situation where the system fails you. Seeing Gerson really, really shook me and I thought about things I hadn’t thought about in a long time – that feeling of helplessness.”

On 18 July 2026 Turcios had been in detention for a full year. His fundraiser has reached more than $130,000 in donations from 1,121 different people, but his legal fight continues. After nine years living in Rhinebeck, Henoch self-deported back to Honduras. He says that, given what was happening to Latino people in the US under the Trump administration, he decided it was better to return. “Having to start over here in Honduras is tough, but it has to be done,” he tells me. Today he works on a cattle farm. Henoch’s former girlfriend, Yorleny Weigel, still lives in Rhinebeck.

She misses Turcios. “I used to take him everywhere with me. People thought he was my son. I’d tell them he wasn’t, but in the end I just gave up and went with it. He loved to go dancing; he’d try to dance but he wasn’t very good.” She talks to Turcios most nights on the phone. “He’s changed,” she says. “He doesn’t want to admit it, but I think it’s breaking him a little bit.”

Today, now aged 24, Turcios is housed in the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn – the same building in which former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and Luigi Mangione, accused of murdering UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York City, are awaiting trial. Immigration detainees are kept separate, but are in the same facility.

Turcios says he’s locked in his cell three times a day but allowed out for breakfast, lunch and dinner, and a few hours’ recreation – playing cards, watching TV. “There are four telephones in the unit and we need to line up to use them,” he says. “Sometimes there are eight people waiting and you don’t get to make a call.”

He says the food is bad – breakfast is a packet of milk and a muffin; lunch is pasta with meat that is “old or cold and flavourless”; dinner is mashed potato, spinach and occasionally chicken. “We don’t see sunshine,” he says. “There is a small room where we play basketball and there’s a big opening like a cage, with no glass, and we can see a little piece of the sky.” He speaks to his parents, Irma and Juan, once a week, but calls are expensive – $10 to call Honduras.

Turcios often thinks about how Trump campaigned on deporting all criminal undocumented immigrants. “But the criminals are on the outside,” he says. “And inside, most of these people here with me just came to the United States to work, to try to build our lives and make things better.”

He wants to return to his home in Rhinebeck. “I knew the community was full of incredible, nice people,” Turcios says. “I never expected everyone would get together to help me out. I was so surprised and happy.”

Turcios’s lawyers are challenging his prolonged detention – under a supreme court ruling, the government may detain someone it wants to deport who has a final order of removal for 90 days; between 90 and 180 days, it must show special justification to keep holding them; and after 180 days, it must prove they are “wildly dangerous”. Copeland says this is a level that even a history of gang-related homicide has in the past failed to meet. He argues that Turcios should have been released by October, roughly 90 days into his detention, and that ICE failed to properly notify him of a custody review hearing. In addition, Copeland is pursuing Turcios’s claim for asylum in the US.

Meanwhile, Turcios’s high school friend Anna Lawson, who recently graduated from McGill University in Canada and is taking a gap year before starting law school, is in disbelief that Turcios has been identified by her government as someone who doesn’t belong here. “Gerson is someone who is a benefit to our community and has only enriched it and helped people. I think the American dream really does live in him. He is such an embodiment of what it’s supposed to mean.”
